REQUEST MEASURES BE TAKEN TO HAVE DAIRY YEAR
subsubtopic: CORRESPOND TO CALENDAR YEAR-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask for the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion concerning a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Since 25 per cent of milk producers will not have any revenues until the end of the dairy year because their quotas have expired and since milk producers must now pay all year long $1.35 for every hundredweight of industrial milk for the storage of powdered milk, which is a very substantial sum when we consider the financial hardship that these people are experiencing, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Lambert):
That the House urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to call immediately for a meeting of the Standing Committee on Agriculture to take an in-depth look at the dairy policy in Canada, a policy that proved disastrous for milk producers in general, so that steps can be taken as soon as possible in order that the dairy year correspond to the calendar year, a step which would have the effect of allowing milk producers to better manage their production volume.

speechtext:

In view of the intense regional antagonism that is developing over the anti-dumping tribunal decision to uphold the Algoma appeal for the imposition of a 30 per cent dumping duty on wide-flange steel beams entered through the port of Vancouver, and in view of the fact that Canadian National Railways, Canadian Pacific Railway and Algoma Central Railways have announced a further increase of 5 per cent on steel rail freight rates from Ontario commencing April 1, 1978, at the expense of western Canada, thus exhibiting an indifference and a failure to adjust the system to allow regional resource-based industries to exist, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen):
That the government of Canada invoke section 7 of the Anti-dumping Act exempting wide-flange steel beams 25 inches and less from the act when imported through the port of Vancouver.

subsubtopic: REQUEST PRIME MINISTER UNDERTAKE RESPONSIBILITIES OF SOLICITOR GENERAL-APPLICATION OF FEDERAL COURT ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the right hon. gentleman a question about what I believe-and I believe many would agree with me-is an unprecedented situation in the administration of justice in this country. With three former solicitors general now not available for questioning in accordance with parliamentary rules, with three judicial inquiries going on respecting the business of the department, and with important legislation pending which is also affecting the portfolio, will the Prime Minister fill this ministerial and parliamentary vacuum by devoting his personal attention to some of these matters, and will he perhaps elaborate later on motions what he plans to do to make certain that the administration of justice in this country does not fail the confidence of the Canadian people?

subsubtopic: REQUEST PRIME MINISTER UNDERTAKE RESPONSIBILITIES OF SOLICITOR GENERAL-APPLICATION OF FEDERAL COURT ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have appointed a royal commission of inquiry to look into allegations of possible improprieties or illegalities committed by representatives of the Canadian government in the administration of justice. We expect this commission of inquiry to search into every relevant aspect of the question. I believe that this is the proper procedure to ensure that the examination of these facts and allegations is not in the hands of the government but, rather, is in the hands of a royal commission of inquiry.

subsubtopic: REQUEST PRIME MINISTER UNDERTAKE RESPONSIBILITIES OF SOLICITOR GENERAL-APPLICATION OF FEDERAL COURT ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest to the Prime Minister that he cannot, in all conscience, delegate all the responsibilities implicit in this House to a royal commission, however eminent. This section, as the Prime Minister knows, sanctions executive privilege without judicial review. I am wondering if the Prime Minister recognizes this fact and is prepared to take steps to change it, particularly in view of the less than positive assurances yesterday of the Minister of Justice that some of the material withheld under the section, without benefit of judicial review, may not necessarily have been in the personal purview and knowledge of the minister who withheld the material.

This, of the proponents, can be questioned: it is the opposition's role to ask questions, if they wish.

speechtext:
In accordance with the government's policy of encouraging a strong and viable agricultural sector, the
January 31, 1978

Income Tax Act was amended in 1973 and 1975 in order to permit farmland, buildings and machinery to be transferred tax-free to a farmer's wife or children on his death. This is generally referred to as a "rollover" privilege. In order to qualify for the rollover, certain conditions must be satisfied. For example, the property must have been used by the farmer or his family in a farming business. subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1977 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-3, respecting the reorganization of Air
Air Canada
Canada, be read the second time and amendments made by the Senate be concurred in.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1977 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks concerning Bill C-3 which was adopted by the House of November 7, 1977, but I do not want to monopolize too much of the time of the House, for the bell has been using up a good part of our time over the past two weeks. If we want to expedite these affairs, we shall have to limit the length of our interventions. I, for one, am quite willing to do so, while making my views known on this bill.
We all recall that the other place studied this bill after it was passed by the House, as I said, and recommended some amendments which, to me, seem valid and which lead me to believe that they will complete it. Such are the aims of Bill C-3. Air Canada is a Crown corporation. As such, all Canadians are shareholders, and directors are appointed to manage the corporation on behalf of all Canadians. Canadians therefore have the right to demand that its directors do their utmost to properly manage this Crown corporation, and to strive for budgetary balance, as do all private companies. That is why we must occasionally come back on this subject here in the House to remind the directors what parliament and Canadians expect of them. They must absolutely manage the corporation without counting too much on government intervention and on parliament's allocating votes to the corporation to restore budgetary balance when it is in the red. I hold this to be a principle of sound management.
The recommendations of the Auditor General of Canada in other areas should also apply to the Crown corporation, Air Canada. Mr. Speaker, it happens sometimes while travelling throughout the country on Air Canada planes that as parliamentarians we ask ourselves some questions as we see their operations. Although we cannot properly query the officials at work, just the same we ask ourselves the following question: Why such and such a thing is done in such and such a way? When we get the reports of the corporation, several questions still remain unanswered. On the other hand, there are some competitive private companies. It is a good thing to have some competition even in that area where private companies do their utmost to provide excellent services to attract customers.
So, for its part, Air Canada must also do what it can to try and attract the greatest number of people to travel on its flights so they will be as full as possible and profitable. But it so happens sometimes, Mr. Speaker, and I do want to draw the attention of the minister on this-although he may be out, perhaps temporarily, I would like to tell him that I noticed on several occasions, and I remember the time when the late Real Caouette used to sit in this House and make rather frequent remarks about the fact that all across Canada the staff on Air Canada planes did not provide adequate bilingual services. I think that with aircraft flying all over this country, if bilingualism is to be promoted in this country Air Canada should have at least bilingual staff on its aircraft. Nothing aggravates me more than when I address an Air Canada employee in French and that employee does not seem to understand me and tells me, I am sorry.

Air Canada
I understand that they should be sorry about it but the fact still remains that I do not get an answer. That is disappointing on an airline such as Air Canada when there would be a great opportunity of setting a good example all across this country and showing that Canada is bilingual and that at least public services are provided in both official languages. We can do that if we really want to. The same thing goes for an Englishspeaking Canadian. Imagine an English-speaking Canadian in Quebec city talking to an Air Canada official at the Ancienne-Lorette airport, the Quebec city airport, and there is no one to answer him in English. He too is going to be aggravated. He is going to wonder: But what is going on in Canada? How come I cannot get service in my language?
That is why I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), who is responsible in this area, to use with his officials all the means he can to try and improve this service in the area of language communication so all Canadians will be proud when they travel on Air Canada planes, if they cannot get it on the ground, to have at least bilingualism in the air. We are going to fight for that, Mr. Speaker. We are going to fight further because it is a right, and because it is part of our constitution. Let us at least live up to the good parts in our Canadian constitution. Some are mere nonsense, but that is something relevant, it is acceptable, it is something we should live up to and be proud of. That would be the best way to ensure understanding between French- and English-speaking Canadians. Looking at each other we look reasonable. But when we try to talk to each other, we do not speak the same language and that is where the problem starts. To help solve the problem we have government services that can very well promote bilingualism, and Air Canada should be an expert in that field.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, on a somewhat more optimistic and very patriotic tone, I must say that when I stand in a foreign airport I am very proud to see our Air Canada aircraft arriving, those giant airplanes with a beautiful flag on their wings. Yes, I feel proud that our planes measure up with those of any other country. They are very well built and very comfortable, and they lack only one thing, bilingualism!
I therefore hope, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is not forgetting this: we demand bilingualism in air services, and we will go on demanding it as long as a favourable answer is not forthcoming. To conclude, I accept the amendments to Bill C-3 and also the bill itself of the proponents. If there is a vote, I shall make a point of supporting it.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1977 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a privilege to say a few words on this piece of legislation, Bill C-3, respecting Air Canada, because ever since I came to this place I have been interested in the operations of our national air line.
I think it is fair to say that during the past two or three years there has been an improvement in the operations of Air Canada, and I think this piece of legislation is a good one and

will facilitate the operations of the company. However, I think that to put matters in a historical perspective it would be useful to go back a little bit, as my friend, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), did yesterday, and to point out some of the delays and some of the incredible lack of inititative by the government in not bringing this legislation forward years ago. I say that advisedly in view of the unfortunate remarks of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) who sought to give the completely inaccurate impression in the program "The Nation's Business" that it was the opposition parties which were holding up the legislative progress of this parliament rather than the government's poor planning and lack of purpose and direction.
I think it is rather amazing to consider that it is now practically six years since the then minister of transport, now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), recognized in this Chamber the urgent need for legislation to revamp and restructure Air Canada. On March 14, 1972 he said:
-I propose to bring before the House in the next session three important pieces of legislation on which work is proceeding at the present time. The first of these is a bill designed to reconstitute Air Canada as a separate Crown corporation, thus divorcing it, as it were, from CNR-
Here we are six years later and, as the saying goes, definitely "it ain't performance". It is almost equally noteworthy that almost three years after the date of the judicial inquiry into certain aspects of Air Canada-an inquiry, as most hon. members realize, for which our party was responsible-we still have not completed, and we are here today trying to complete, the legislative process to embody some of the changes and improvements recommended by Mr. Justice Estey in that report.
Part of the problem has been the reluctance to accept some of the logic and reason that has been put forward from many sources until the government was practically coerced into doing so. Even the noteworthy section which the minister and his colleagues have finally agreed to eliminate, section 6(2), has been eliminated only after the other place-and I think they deserve credit for this-reinforced this party's determination to take away this carte blanche which the government sought to have which, in my view, would seriously undermine the integrity of this legislation.
I think it would be useful to go back a little way since there have been developments so far as our national air line is concerned which indicate that there is a possibility that Nor-dair will be acquired, and to point out that just as the progress has been tortuously slow in respect of this particular piece of needed legislation, the policy with respect to regionals has been, if anything, even slower.
In October, 1966, J. W. Pickersgill, who was then minister of transport, issued a statement of principles outlining the role the regional air lines would be committed to play. They were to provide regular route operations into the north, and to operate local and regional routes to complement the main carriers. Where appropriate, routes operated by the mainline companies would be transferred to the regionals.
January 31, 1978

There were other developments which were proposed by the government at that time. The Air Transport Board, now the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission, would be responsible for deciding which routes would be suitable for regional air line operations; it would also administer the policy relating to the transfer of these routes.
The regional carriers accepted this policy and began to develop their operations within its framework. They had long recognized the need to increase traffic and improve the stability of their operations, but had been hesitant to do so without firm recognition and direction from government. Under the new policy, they were prepared to move on their own initiative to develop their scheduled service, seek out new routes, and use their own resources, imagination, and business acumen to make them profitable. That has not happened very quickly.
In 1969 the government announced a refinement of the policy, dividing the country into regions and letting the regional know exactly where they could move. Pacific Western was given British Columbia and western Alberta; Transair the prairie provinces and northwestern Ontario, and so on. Nor-dair and other regionals were given certain route structures.
The policy allowed for route transfers, modest competition with the mainline carriers, and co-operation between the two.
The Air Transport Committee has taken no action of any consequence, so far as I know, to determine which routes operated by the mainline carriers are eligible for transfer. No guidelines have yet been developed for new types of services that could be established by regional carriers, services such as airbus or specialized cargo services, with few if any exceptions.
Co-operation between the mainline carriers on route transfers to regional carriers has not been consistent. The eight years or so that have passed since some of these policies were announced have been noteworthy because of the mushrooming of the so-called third-level carriers. These carriers are smaller than regional carriers, which are also looking upward and outward. I suggest that these reasons make it necessary and a matter of some urgency to re-examine some of the objectives envisioned by the policy and to ensure their early realization.
Surely Canada now needs, in the context of the legislation we are dealing with today, a clear policy statement on transcontinental, regional, third-level, helicopter and charter operations, if our air transportation system is to continue to grow in an orderly way.
Our national carrier recently has been doing much better financially, but in order to keep matters in perpective we must realize that profitability alone can never be the sole criterion for a national air carrier, otherwise there will be very justifiable concerns raised by the disadvantaged parts of the country which rightly expect our national air carrier to help facilitate regional development.
Before we get too puffed up about the profits Air Canada is expected to show, I think we should remember that some of its competitors in North America, particularly in the United
Air Canada
States, face tougher competition. Some competitors have roughly comparable route structures but are doing much better. They are doing so with fewer employees and lesser load factors. The annual report of Delta Airlines, which I have before me, indicates that for the year 1977 Delta's profit before taxes was $155 million, and it appears that its net profit will be over $90 million. I have heard a figure of possibly $20 million for Air Canada, which is certainly much better than its performance in recent years, but when that is compared with the performance of Delta we realize that, while it is reasonable, it is not something Air Canada can necessarily point to with any overweening pride.
It seems to me that there are some legitimate questions to raise about the situation in which Nordair is in the process of being acquired by Air Canada. My colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville, discussed this situation yesterday, and I want to touch upon some of the things he said.
It is pretty obvious that Air Canada has not been particularly imaginative or innovative in getting into the charter business or in developing new route structures. I well remember the abortive experience this company had when it tried to acquire Wardair and the rather naive way the corporate expertise of Air Canada stacked up against the much more practical and knowledgeable expertise shown by this particular private charter carrier. In the present particular case Nordair is a pretty healthy and well respected regional carrier, and I would have thought that if Air Canada was going to pick up a regional carrier, it would have been the better policy to take one with some financial difficulty. That would have rationalized the system somewhat and would have had the virtue of rescuing a carrier which perhaps needed help. However, what do we see with respect to Nordair? It is probably one of the healthiest-at least recently-regional carriers.
It is interesting that the proposed price of $ 11.50 for each Nordair share is $4.50 more than the price the stock was trading at when the exchange closed late in December of last year, a matter of a very few weeks ago. It is also interesting, although far be it from me to knock private enterprise, that some of the main shareholders of Nordair are going to make some very substantial profits. It appears that this may be done at the expense, indirectly at least, of the taxpayers of Canada, who are the ultimate owners of Air Canada. Mr. Tooley appears to be headed for a profit of $1 million in a very short time, based on the market fluctuations of the stock. Mr. Marx, one of the principal shareholders who lives in New York, picked up 17,000 shares at $2.58 per share last June. Now he is going to get $11.50, a nice little profit indeed.
Apart from that there is concern in the industry about the effect this may have on the relationship of other regional carriers. According to the Montreal Star the president of Pacific Western Airlines, Mr. Eyton, is concerned. According to an article in the Montreal Star of January 10 of this year, Air Canada's purchase of the Montreal-based Nordair Limited may interfere with his company's plans.

January 31, 1978
Air Canada
Mr. Eyton was quoted as follows:
I would not like to see a regional carrier like PWA running alongside a major carrier like Air Canada. With the acquisition of Nordair any route opportunities, in terms of what Air Canada might have been willing to turn over to regional carriers, is lost.
From an historical perspective it is interesting how things turn out, because if Air Canada had directed its attention to its own corporate business as much as to opposing some of the regional carriers like, ironically enough, the one it now seeks to acquire, we would all be better off. In the not so recent past our national airline opposed Nordair in its application for routes, and I am thinking particularly of the Montreal-Ottawa-Sudbury-Thunder Bay route. Now we find that this company is gobbling up, or acquiring at the expense of the taxpayers of this country, what it opposed and what it was not able to develop by itself a very short time ago.
I want to say at this time again that in making these remarks I am not taking an anti-Air Canada bias. I very much hope that our national air carrier does well. I personally have high regard for the chief executive officer, and I am particularly impressed with the morale and efficiency of many of the employees. As the hon. member for Vegreville said yesterday, it is a shame that the proposed reward by way of a bonus involving passes to employees was handled in a rather peremptory and perhaps not very efficient way, which probably has the net effect of embarrassing the employees and blunting an initiative which might have been very appropriate had it been handled in a slightly different way after some consultations and some variations, instead of having the announcement made and then having to vary the original proposal.
Another thing I think we have to look at is the fact that, as far as I am concerned, Air Canada is not fulfilling its mandate in the eastern part of the country in the sense of serving as a real aid to developing that part of the country and providing it with important links. Surely there must be something Air Canada and the government can do to facilitate the utilization of the route from Halifax to Bangor.
In 1973 Canada and the United States signed a bilateral agreement which included a route, effective as of January 1, 1974, between Montreal, Bangor, Portland and Halifax. This route has never been implemented because, according to Air Canada, there was no money in it. The route was designated to be of use only in summer peak service periods. I understand that Air Canada is now saying that that was the time in 1974 when the airline industry was in an upheaval crisis due to fuel shortages. I also understand, although it has not been officially confirmed, that Air Canada would consider the possibility of subcontracting or negotiating this route with some other air carrier.
However, be that as it may, it seems obvious that Bangor is making great strides as a commercial and warehousing centre in the northeastern part of the United States. It is obvious to anyone who knows the maritime provinces that Halifax is becoming more and more a commercial centre for that region of the country.

The Halifax International Airport was recently upgraded. I should like to see the Ottawa International Airport given the same kind of facilities that Halifax now has. At the present time when one boards an aircraft at Ottawa airport it is like going on a tour of the sunken gardens or a sideshow orientation where you go through long winding tunnels and canvass flaps of various hues. I guess improvements will come in time.
The Halifax-Bangor route ought to be developed. I am no expert on air transportation but I imagine any route that requires promotion and pioneering will lose money for a while. I also imagine that, if Air Canada does not do something constructive soon, residents of this area will be justified in asking their elected representatives to consider allowing an airline like Delta to operate there-one that is already making at least four times the profit of Air Canada and under tougher competition.
I think it should be made clear to the chief executive officers of the airline and to the government that if they do not do something about filling this designated route with a Canadian air carrier that can provide needed transportation and trade links with Bangor, an American carrier should be permitted and even encouraged to come in and do the job. This has to be considered.
In summing up my views about this legislation I must say the thing that must be kept in mind is that it would appear that this bill seems to have achieved the objective of giving Air Canada enough corporate freedom and initiative to do its job without interference from officials in the Department of Transport who have a penchant for fouling up everything they attempt and antagonising people at the same time, at least at the highest levels. It also seems to have had the effect of giving the board of directors a clear mandate. The primary objective, of the proponents, was to free this billion dollar corporation of the entanglements that our other national carrier, the CNR, has experienced.
Members of this House will be watching very closely to see the beneficial effects of this legislation and will expect the minister and his cabinet colleagues to ensure that the improved framework for operating the airline is used properly.
I urge the government to cease the practice which has been so painfully evident in the past of scheduling-or not scheduling-committee proceedings so that Air Canada can be reviewed regularly by interested elected representatives. It is not the fault of our national air carrier that their appearances before the transportation committee have been few and far between; it is rather due to the ineptitude and bungling of the government. As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, the government has attempted to place the responsibility for this on the shoulders of the opposition parties. The government House leader will be sorry, I am sure, for the representation that he put over the networks of this country as it is so self-serving and so false.
The legislation could be summed up in the words of an old proverb-better late than never. I trust it will serve our
January 31, 1978

national air carrier well and justify the work and concern that so many members of this House from all parties have put into its composition.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1977 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Order, please. The Chair would like to point out to all hon. members that we have been very lenient with members who have spoken on Bill C-3 dealing with amendments made by the other place. I would therefore suggest that all future speakers stay strictly on the flight path and speak only on those technical amendments made by the other place.
I should like to refer hon. members to May's eighteenth edition, page 534, where the following passage appears:
The debate on this motion must be confined to the amendment under consideration, and may not extend to other amendments or to the general merits of the bill.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1977 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I presume it was purely accidental that you made your ruling at this particular time. After listening to some of the other speeches I do not see how I could possibly be out of order.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) must be interested that we are now having another kick at the cat because of the sober second thought given this bill in the other place. Some of my colleagues disagree with the word "sober" but that word appears in the legislation which created the other place. The amendments have eliminated the right of the government to make decisions. Instead of being covered by order in council, they are now to be covered by order of the governor in council.
One of the major changes that Air Canada has made recently is that the president is no longer a political appointee but rather is someone who has risen from the ranks. This would appear to be a good measure judging by the fact that in 1975 the airline lost over $13 million while in the first quarter of 1977 it showed a profit. We appreciate the good job done by the president, Mr. Claude Taylor, and all previous speakers have referred to this.
A former minister of transport, Senator Marchand, when speaking on this bill, referred to the great size of this country and the difference in services necessary for different parts of it and to the fact that heavily populated areas require a different transportation facility than that necessary for remote areas. Of the proponents that was recognized when the country was founded and when assistance was given to the Canadian Pacific Railway to provide facilities in remote areas.
Air travel in this country started with a large number of very small airlines, one man-one plane operations, and eventually we established what we hoped would be the flag-fleet of the air service of Canada to carry our flag all over the world. Members who have travelled abroad have been very proud to see an Air Canada plane sitting at an airport in Europe, Asia, Africa, or any other part of the world. This equals the pride which the people of France have in Air France, and the British have in their airlines serving all parts of the world. I am sure this is true of every country. It is also interesting to note the pride of small African countries in their airlines. When travelling from central Africa to England, they take great pride in
Air Canada
flying the banner of East African Airlines. This pride is worth something.
Over the years Canada has been well served by Air Canada. However, Air Canada has had a great deal of problems. We have never had a transportation facility which takes into consideration the fact that if it is going to operate all across this country, providing service on uneconomic routes to the by-ways of the nation, it must use income derived from the heavily populated routes to provide such service.
It has been pointed out that we have not been able to compete. Neither have the railways. They have not been able to compete in the United States. A few moments ago, an hon. member referred to Delta Airlines. In the United States there are eight or ten airlines. They have a population of 220 million on which to draw. In Canada there are seven main carriers, five regionals and two major airlines, Air Canada and CP. We have a population of only 22 million. I believe we have done very well.
It is interesting to note the way the American airlines have changed their accounting system. For example, in one year Eastern Airlines lost $45 million. The next year they had a book transfer of $44 million. Therefore they are now able to show a profit. They may not be able to do that over a ten-year period. Eventually they will have to relate to the new book values they have placed on their investment. That will have to be taken into consideration.
Despite bad management of Air Canada and the fact the government treated it as having a responsibility without offsetting it with any asset, Air Canada has done fairly well. In 1975 Air Canada had a loss of $13 million. It reached the point where morale was rock bottom.
I recall members of this House asking for a financial statement. The situation was so bad at that time the government could not decide whether to honour the previous government's commitment to an auditing firm to audit the books of Air Canada or whether to appoint their own auditors. For a number of years there were no auditors because the government could not resolve that problem. They operated under immense hardship. The morale of Air Canada suffered badly. Mr. Claude Taylor has been able to make great changes. Therefore, we must give him the support that is necessary. This will involve a number of things.
The Minister of Transport stated, and I am paraphrasing, that his purpose is to get Air Canada into a position where it is making money and is a financial success. If that is achieved, the minister thinks we should then get rid of those sections that are successful. In my opinion, Air Canada would be fragmented to the point where it would be in the same position as the CN passenger service.
Not long ago I attended one of railway hearings. I am sure Your Honour has been at many of them. The CNR was asking for subsidization of passenger service on a specific line. That was the only question before the hearing, whether they should be allowed to drop passenger service on that line which ran

January 31, 1978
Air Canada
between North Bay and Toronto. I attended as a member of parliament. I completely supported their application to drop that passenger service. I was opposed to a subsidy being paid to them when they were not in effect operating a service. Service was so bad that no one would use it. People use the Ontario Northland Railway, a totally Ontario-owned railway which operates in this province. That railway is not entitled to apply for a subsidy. CN asked for a subsidy or, in the alternative, to drop the service.
I had hoped that CN would sell its line to Ontario Northland so that passenger service between northern Ontario and Toronto could become more efficient. I am sure it could be operated without a loss. There would be no need for a subsidy. But of the proponents, it was decided that CN must continue, and because it had to continue, they were to be subsidized.
From reading the bill and the changes recommended by the other place, my understanding is that Air Canada will be permitted to implement a regional basis of reporting. Recently, Transair was told to take the western Canadian routes from Winnipeg to Regina, Winnipeg to Edmonton and Winnipeg to Calgary. These routes are now operating at a loss. In return for that, they were given the route from Winnipeg to Toronto through Thunder Bay and Sault Ste. Marie. As a result of transfers like this, airlines will be fragmented to the point that it will be impossible to travel anywhere in Canada without travelling on two or three different carriers. If this operates like a railroad, and I have every reason to believe it does, we will find that the initiating line, which will likely be between the major operating centres, will get the lion's share of the revenues. Very little will be left for the carriers that operate on a regional basis.
Your Honour is very fortunate to be in the position where you can fly from here to your constituency on one airline, the government airline. If I fly to my constituency, I must travel on two airlines. And even if I take the alternative to the Air Canada route, I must travel on two airlines as well.
If the profitable runs are sold, I suggest that it will be necessary to make two or three changes when travelling in this country. This means giving up the idea of a national airline with equal opportunity to people living in various parts of the country. This is a fundamental right to which Canadians are entitled.
Air Canada is being told to fly into Yellowknife. For years I travelled on a route which lost money. It went from Montreal to Ottawa, Ottawa to Val-d'Or, Val-d'Or to Rouyn, Rouyn to Earlton, on to Toronto and then back to Montreal. The mileage on that one flight would cover half the distance of travelling to Europe. There were many stops on that run. The passenger service was not sufficient to cover the cost of operation of that run. However, it filled a great need for the people of northern Quebec and northeastern Ontario.
I am sure that every member who lives outside of the five or six major centres is aware of what Air Canada did for the citizens of this country, even though it was not economically advantageous. However, they felt they had a right to some service.

I would be remiss if I did not refer to something which has been mentioned many times by other members in relation to the American airlines. Along with other airlines Air Canada made the mistake especially in the late sixties, of getting the wrong type of aircraft for many of the routes it was serving. It was almost commonplace to see routes served by aircraft which were never more than half filled. It seems to me this is why the regional carriers are successful-they have been willing to buy aircraft which meet the needs of these runs.
I am flying almost regularly now, in 1978, in a DC-3 which was virtually obsolete in the middle forties, a plane which has not been modified or changed in any substantial way since the forties. It was flying in the thirties and it is still flying. I consider the Douglas DC-3 to be one of the safest planes we have. It is true it lacks some of the advantages of modern planes but it can carry passengers more economically on a cents-per-mile basis than most modern aircraft, and it meets the needs of routes where only a light passenger load can be expected.
It is unfortunate that Air Canada did not see fit to acquire a certain number of smaller aircraft so that it could move passengers along such routes in a more economical way. I have no doubt the management of the corporation will be giving close consideration to this aspect. I trust no decision will be made to buy Twin Otters for no better reason than to keep the investments of the Ontario government or of the federal government safe. It seems to me we should be buying aircraft on a totally different basis.
Many airlines in the United States operated with Viscount aircraft, probably the most expensive passenger aircraft ever developed. They were so expensive that two or three of the U.S. airlines using them went bankrupt. It took a very rich organization, Air Canada, to operate the Viscount during its last years of service. The correct choice of aircraft is a matter of great importance, it seems to me.
With perhaps one exception, the bill has come back to us from the Senate with very little alteration. Apart from clause 8, most of the amendments merely involve renumbering clauses. I have a copy of a note sent along with the amendments and signed by James Lyon, acting general counsel for the Department of Finance. I imagine that some of the amendments were made at the instigation of the Department of Finance since they involve technical matters which might have been overlooked in the original drafting.
One new subclause added by the Senate was to the effect that an order of the governor in council made under clause 6 or clause 8 must be tabled in parliament and published in the Canada Gazette. This is an amendment with which I am sure all members agree. I presume that all orders in council make their way in time into the Canada Gazette, but I would point out that the Canada Gazette is no longer a publication which is read by the average Canadian, though it might interest lawyers and members of legislatures across the country, as well as a handful of other persons who follow these matters closely.
January 31, 1978

I am sure most hon. members have read this publication from time to time and found very little in it which was exciting or illuminating; after reading it for a while and failing to understand what was in it, most of us have desisted from that exercise. If, on the other hand, an order in council is tabled in the House of Commons, interest is immediately attracted. I see my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre is fidgeting in his place. He probably wants to make the point that people are not likely to pay close attention to orders which are tabled in the House, either-of the proponents, that does not apply to me! I see that Senator Grosart and Senator Forsey read them, and if somebody reads them it is likely that orders in council which provoke disagreement will be brought to the attention of the House.
Many of the changes which are made by order in council are carried out because some departmental official finds them to be to his advantage. So a change is made in the form, the direction, or, sometimes, even in the content of legislation. I am sure members of parliament want to know about these things so I believe it is safe to say everyone will support the provision for the tabling of these particular orders in council in the House. After all, the changes might be extensive.
At some point in time, possibly after further study, the government may wish to break off a particular section of the corporation's activities without harming the remaining operations. Those sections which become profitable will be sold and it might be possible to make such changes on the basis of clause 6 of the bill which sets out the powers and activities of the corporation, allowing it to buy, sell, lease, hire, dispose of, maintain, operate and so on. The corporation is by no means restricted to the operation of aircraft. It can provide hotels, surface vehicles and other facilities for servicing and housing. Any single one of these operations, if it became viable, might be broken off. One of the first the minister might consider would be Econo-Travel, the travel service which has been operating for years with mixed success.
It may be Air Canada will want to build hotels as other airlines have done in countries such as in the Caribbean. They may want to build them in France. In travelling to France, Canadians are at a very great disadvantage. In travelling to Paris, particularly if you fly Air France, you can stay at a very reduced rate at hotels owned by Air France. However, if you fly by Air Canada you cannot get that same kind of an arrangement.
We are attempting, I presume, to do the same kind of business which we have done over the years unsuccessfully with CN. It may be by order in council that we may be able to commence building facilities of various kinds, ancillary services, and when they become viable enterprises and stand on their own two feet they will be sold. It may be they will be sold, under the direction of an order in council, and the disposition may be able to be made under clause 6 of this bill.
The Senate, Mr. Speaker, were also concerned about a number of other amendments, all very consequential on the
Air Canada
passing of the initial one, with one exception that stands on its own. The Senate intend by many of these amendments, and there are quite a number of them, just to change the numbering of the clauses. While it is necessary, I think it might have been possible if this House passed the first one we would have known ourselves of the necessity to change the numbering, or there would have been two numbers for the same clause. We do end up with a lot of amendments which we may want to go through at another stage. However, I think at this stage we should be more interested in whether we want to pass the major amendments in this bill. They will in effect change the method used in these acquisitions, disposals and operations of all the ancillary services which I am not sure properly belong to an airline, but which we have created as part of our Canadian airline.
I believe this bill gives the government more power, and in my opinion the airlines should be worried about this as well. Mr. Taylor is a very outspoken gentleman and, I am sure, far-seeing. He will undoubtedly see the disadvantage of the cabinet deciding whether or not Transair should have the right to make the $12 million exchange from the Toronto-Thunder Bay-Winnipeg run to runs including Winnipeg, Regina-the local prairie runs. If the cabinet makes these decisions, Mr. Taylor, I presume, will not be with us very long and we will return to a much more unsatisfactory management. As I see it, Mr. Speaker, these changes can be made in that manner, and we are very concerned.
I personally do not think that there is anything wrong with the initial purpose of Air Canada in providing reasonable transportation to all Canadians, no matter where they live, where it is at all feasible, and where the cost is not exorbitant and prohibitive. In the main, Air Canada has been willing to do this. We have certainly attached to them a terrific handicap. Certainly the Conservatives should be blamed for this handicap because they allowed Canadian Pacific, as an alternate airline, to pick up the cream of the runs, and not to do anything for Canada, not to do anything for the unity of this nation. Canadian Pacific Airlines do not travel to any place which does not pay them to go there. They do not operate anything that it does not pay them to operate. They are a truly private enterprise operation, and I have no quarrel with that. If 1 were a shareholder of Canadian Pacific Airlines I would be very pleased with the way the airline is managed. But, Mr. Speaker, if I were president of Air Canada I would have grave objection to the kind of competition that I meet, which does not aid in the role that I have of providing all Canadians with access to air travel.
1 do not object to competition, but competition should be fair. Competition which the Conservatives speak of is one horse, one rabbit. That may be 50-50, but it is not a very fair 50-50. I believe it should be fair. If we ask the same of our regional carriers, if we ask the same of our two national carriers, that is competition fair and square, and may the best company win.
If Air Canada under those terms could not survive and Canadian Pacific did, then Canadian Pacific would be the flag

January 31, 1978
Air Canada
carrier of our nation. In my opinion that is competition. But what we have today is not competition and I disagree violently with the idea of frittering away little parts because they become profitable, and that appears to be what is going to happen.
One of these amendments questions how this can be done. It questions what the government is doing, and the way the government reports it to parliament. I suggest there are still those in Canada proud of the national airline. Do not forget, Mr. Speaker, many of those people who are proud of Air Canada are proud of it for the simple reason that it is Air Canada. They are proud of its record. They are proud of it because it flies from community to community and carries our flag to other countries around the world. It is not because Canadian people travel via Air Canada. When we provide air travel, we provide it for a very limited number of people in this country. There are people who travel on an air carrier almost every day of their work week, but most people save up all year, take one trip to go on a holiday somewhere, which is usually outside of the country, and that is the only occasion when they fly.
The average Canadian does not travel by air. It is too expensive, and his time is not that valuable. He can afford to drive, to ride a bus or take the train. Therefore we always have to keep in mind that we are providing this type of service, which is very necessary for the economy of the nation. It is very necessary transportation for the business of the communities and it is very important for those who have to get from one point to another over a great distance in a short period of time. We are certainly not suggesting it is not important. We should keep in mind it is important, but that it applies to a very small percentage of our population.
In closing, looking at any record of Air Canada and comparing it with American records, Air Canada does not fare too badly. It is interesting to note the traffic growth in the United States. For instance the revenue per passenger mile for airlines increased 9.9 per cent and freight ton miles increased 6.5 per cent. The industry was more productive by increasing its load factor from 53.7 per cent to 55.4 per cent. However, this falls far short of Air Canada's 61 per cent load factor. Traffic growth in Canada was much slower because of the size of our population and the distance between major cities. Between 1975 and 1976 Air Canada increased its revenue passenger miles by 6 per cent, while Canadian Pacific, that great free enterprise, decreased its revenue passenger miles by 1 per cent. Thus, Air Canada is not doing so bad, and it is serving the Canadian public.
The government should make up its mind on what is going to be done with regional carriers and Canadian Pacific. Is Canadian Pacific to the Liberal party what it was to the Conservative party? Is it their little darling? Does it have to be protected? Does it have to be given all kinds of advantages? The former minister of transport, Mr. Marchand, indicated that it is the over-all transportation facility for Canadians.

Will the government look at it in the same way? If Canadian Pacific is to have this great advantage, then we should know about it. It should be put into a position which is not competitive, because it is not competitive compared to Air Canada.
Something should be done about regional carriers. They should be allowed free access to the market, wherever it may be, within their regions. They should be allowed to compete on the national runs, as Canadian Pacific does. The routes should be formalized. We should take the bull by the horns in terms of travel in Canada, which has been mentioned by other hon. members.
When one can travel to the Caribbean and Mexico and pay less than $400 for a hotel room for a week, and in some cases for two weeks, and when it costs $400 for a person to fly from Ottawa to Vancouver, then surely there is something wrong with the suggestion that a service is being provided to Canadians. If those arrangements are available outside Canada, surely they can be arranged inside Canada.
I do not think the government believes in national unity. It believes in keeping Quebec in the Liberal party. It would be nice for the people of the maritimes to be able to travel to Vancouver for less than $500, and vice versa. Canadians should be given a break when travelling across this country. I have been on planes travelling across Canada which have been slightly over half full. Surely a break could be given to people in order for them to see Canada, especially if they cannot travel otherwise, even if it requires staying in hotels over night on a standby basis to allow normal revenue passengers to take their flights. If we do not intend to do that, then we are only paying lip service to national unity.
My friends across Canada who work in factories, mines, and forests receive only two weeks for their holidays. In order for them to drive to British Columbia and back, they require ten days. Thus, they are left with four days to visit the provinces which they pass through. The only way they can see Canada, which would provide them with a better understanding of the problems facing the country, would be a lesser air fare. The Senate amendments may make it possible for the government to do this, but I have seen little indication on the part of the government that it wants to serve such a role. Rather, it seems the government wants to serve the conservative role, which seems to be a competitive enterprise system for CP Air and very little for the national flight carrier, Air Canada.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1977 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1977 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments we are studying today include among them an amendment to clause 6.(1 )(g) of the bill, which would give Air Canada the authority to "acquire and hold shares or debt obligations of any other body corporate carrying on activities similar or incidental to those of the corporation and sell or otherwise deal with such shares or debt obligations."
Another amendment we are considering is with respect to clause 6.(2) of the bill which reads as follows:
January 31, 1978

The governor in council may, by order, authorize the corporation to engage in or carry on any activities not otherwise authorized by this act.
There could be concern about the authority to be given directly to the corporation to acquire control of other airline operations, particularly when one takes a preliminary look at the intended takeover by Air Canada of Nordair. Also one can wonder about the implications of the authority which the original bill intended to give to the governor in council. If the amendment from the other place is not accepted, it should be clarified whether this authority would prevail over the regulatory authority of the Canadian Transport Commission.
I am raising this matter at this time in connection with the proposed acquisition of majority control of Nordair by Air Canada. Because of my concerns about this, I have asked the Canadian Transport Commission to make certain, in considering whether to approve the Air Canada takeover of Nordair, that this takeover will not result in any lessening of the service now being provided to Windsor, Hamilton, Ottawa, Montreal and other communities on the present Nordair route by either Nordair or Air Canada. Also I have asked the director of the combines branch of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to use the authority given him by amendments to the Combines Act, which have been in force since 1976, to consider and make representations to the Canadian Transport Commission about the implications for competition in Canada if permission was granted for Air Canada to take over Nordair.
Air Canada and Nordair are the only airlines providing scheduled service to Windsor, Ontario. Nordair is the only airline directly providing scheduled service to Hamilton, Ontario, although I understand Air Canada advertises its service to Malton airport as serving "Toronto-Hamilton". I am sure the people of Hamilton would agree that such service is not the same as serving Hamilton directly via Mount Hope airport as Nordair does.
The existence of the scheduled service by Nordair to Windsor, Hamilton, Ottawa, Montreal, and so on, during the past few years has provided useful competition to Air Canada. It has provided needed additional flights at convenient times to these communities which were not available until Nordair began its scheduled service to them. Also Nordair has been offering special fares for weekends, for senior citizens and young people, which I understand are less costly than equivalent fares offered by Air Canada. It would not be in the best interests of the communities presently served by Nordair if the takeover by Air Canada brings about any decrease in the services presently offered to them by either or both Nordair and Air Canada.
At about the time of the announcement of the offer of Air Canada to acquire the majority control of Nordair press reports suggested that Air Canada was interested in buying Nordair because of the successful business it has built up in charter flights to foreign destinations. The primary objective of Air Canada should be to improve its service offered within Canada and to make it less costly than at present. Air Canada should strive to change the present situation where it is often
Air Canada
cheaper for Canadians to fly outside Canada, even on Canadian airlines, than it is to fly to points within Canada. It would not be in the public interest if Air Canada attempted to increase its charter business to foreign points by used Nordair planes which are presently serving scheduled routes within Canada.
The press reports at the time of the announcement of the intended takeover of Nordair by Air Canada did not indicate in any way that such a step would be necessary in order to keep Nordair operating since it has been reported to have been financially successful in recent years. That is why, as I have said, I have raised this matter with the Canadian Transport Commission and also with the director of the combines branch of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. As a result, I have been informed very recently by Robert J. Bertrand, director of the combines branch, that he is presently examining the proposed acquisition in light of the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act and those of the National Transportation Act. He went on to inform me that his examination is to determine the extent to which competition will be lessened in the provision of air transportation in Canada, and the effect such a transaction will have on competition in other allied service industries.
I hope that the director of the combines branch will soon complete his preliminary examination and confirm that he will use the authority he now has to raise before the Transport Commission the implications for competition in the air line and related industries if the proposed takeover of Nordair by Air Canada is allowed to go through. I am pleased to have his confirmation that, as a result of my bringing the matter to his attention, he has begun reviewing this transaction for that purpose.
A basis for concern about the effects on competition of the takeover if it were allowed to go through is provided by what is said in a letter which Gerry O'Rourke, assistant manager of Arrow Travel Agency Ltd., sent to Mrs. P. Delbridge of the Consumers' Association of Canada. I refer particularly to the following statement, assuming it contains correct information, in the second paragraph of Mrs. O'Rourke's letter, which reads:
Nordair was also contacted for a price which, at the moment, they have to decline quoting until Air Canada either cannot fulfil your request or for some other reason are unable to accept your booking. Once Air Canada has refused, then Nordair will be pleased to give a price.
Mrs. O'Rourke's letter is dated January 18. It is my understanding that the acquisition of a controlling interest in Nordair by Air Canada subject to CTC approval was announced some nine days earlier.
It might be that the Nordair position referred to in Mrs. O'Rourke's letter is consistent with existing regulations, but if this is so, these regulations would seem to be anticompetitive in their impact, and this is a matter which should be considered by the Transport Commission and which should be raised before it by the director of the combines branch.

January 31, 1978
Air Canada
As a result of my expressing my concerns in a preliminary way to the president of the Canadian Transport Commission about the proposed takeover the president, the Hon. E. J. Benson, replied to me that he has forwarded a copy of my letter to the chairman of the Air Transport Committee. He went on to say, in effect, that he assumed I wanted to oppose the acquisition and my letter dated January 9 could therefore be accepted as a letter of opposition as contemplated by section 27 of the act, if this were my wish and intention. I want to inform the House that as a result, I wrote formally to the president of the CTC saying that I wanted to confirm that my letter to him of January 9 should constitute a formal objection to the proposed acquisition. Also in my letter, I requested that the proposed acquisition be the subject of public hearings by the Air Transport Committee of the CTC.
It is interesting to note that it is not obligatory for this type of transaction to be the subject of public hearings, as I think should be the case, but I hope that the Air Transport Committee will accede to my request and that the matter of the approval of the takeover will be the subject of public hearings so that community bodies in Hamilton, Windsor and elsewhere will have a chance to state their views, but I know that they have concerns similar to mine which they have already expressed in local communities.
It is my intention as well to pursue these concerns, but I wanted to raise this matter at this time to indicate how the broad authority which it is intended this bill should give to Air Canada, and which in some ways it already has, could possibly be exercised in a way which is contrary to the best interests of the communities served by both Air Canada and Nordair, a consequence which could have anti-competitive effects. This should be very important to Canada at this time when we want to stimulate competition in all industries in order to bring about the pressures of competition for the well-being of all Canadians.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1977 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, early last October when this Air Canada reorganization bill was before us in the House I made a few brief remarks-I believe it was last November 1-about some very specific aspects of the bill. They dealt with only three items, two of them dealing with the Air Canada freight policy for livestock and a third one dealing with Air Canada's policy of buying off-shore beef, principally from Australia and New Zealand, for their passenger service meals, when we in Canada, through our own Canadian cattle industry, can supply the best beef in the world.
The first two aspects on which I touched were the air freight policy of Air Canada with respect to freighting live cattle and the insistence of Air Canada on the first right of refusal on all bids for air freighting of cattle out of Canada. I do not propose to repeat my earlier remarks on these specific issues, but I know of some new developments since that earlier debate which I would like to touch upon. They do not relate to the same aspects and I want to suggest that this information has come to me principally as a result of being in close co-operation with the only two truly Canadian forwarders of livestock, and particularly cattle, in Canada. One of them is World Wide

Forwarders based in Farnham, Quebec. They have been the leading forwarders not only in Canada but in North America for a number of years. The other one is a new organization known as Alberta-Canada All Breeds Association, which has recently become active and which operates out of Calgary.
Last December 20, just before we recessed, as a result, I am sure, of my earlier remarks and which were quite specific about Air Canada's air freight policy for livestock, I was supplied with a brief directive from Air Canada with limited information. I want to quote from that information. It is in the form of a very brief message and it is dated December 20. It reads:
Air Canada has a fleet of six DC-8 freighters, all of which may be used for cattle charters. On the average, the air line operates some 50 such charters each year and works with CIDA in the export of Canadian livestock.
For more than two years the air line has used the more efficient and humane loading equipment which permits cattle to be "walked" on to the aircraft.
A number of continuing improvements have been effected over the years as a result of regular meeting with owner and forwarder representative associations.
Air Canada's pricing structure for these charters is competitive with other operators.
A postscript at the bottom of that information sheet says the following:
PWA has not been in the cattle charter business for some time due to a reported heavy loss in this market. Also, the normal advance application to the CTC for operation of a cattle charter is 30 days.
That reference to Pacific Western's experience in hauling live cattle with specially equipped aircraft, which that company had at one time, relates to some of my earlier remarks. It is true that that particular service is no longer operating, because evidently PWA chose to get into passenger service with that particular aircraft. That was PWA's decision, but in the short interval PWA was operating that service PWA demonstrated how to load live cattle on to an aircraft and move them very efficiently. PWA developed the best possible system, and that system is still used by some carriers. It is truly a walk-on system whereby the cattle walk off a cattle liner, up the appropriate chute and right into the aircraft where there are appropriate cross pens in which to contain them.
I want to make some remarks about the message I received. I am sure the information statement was prepared in answer to those earlier remarks of mine. As a result of information I received from World Wide Forwarders operating out of Quebec, it is my understanding that representatives of Air Canada say they are using a walk-on system at Mirabel, but I have gone to some trouble to learn that the situation is simply that they still use a crate system, at least for lighter cattle. I have not been able to find out what they do for heavier cattle, but they insist on a crating system whereby the cattle are loaded into temporary, flimsy crates. They are lifted by forklift high enough to be pushed into the fuselage of the aircraft on a dolly system. After they are inside, they are released, and they walk into the various compartments. That is what Air Canada
January 31, 1978

calls a walk-on system, which is a less than adequate explanation.
As I explained, a true walk-on system is much more efficient. By having the cattle walk off a cattle liner, through an appropriate chute and up into the aircraft it is possible to load a large aircraft in perhaps no more than an hour, or an hour and ten minutes at the most. One can appreciate the extra cost involved in holding up a large aircraft which sometimes requires up to five or six hours to load using the much less efficient system of using crates and forklifts. I was informed that the only time Air Canada used a true walk-on system was when there were snowplowing problems at Mirabel. Arrangements were made to load an aircraft at Dorval. The other system was used, and the operation was much more efficient.
I would like to comment on the statement that Air Canada's pricing structure for these charters is competitive with other operations. I suggest most sincerely that Air Canada is not competitive, especially with regard to large cattle. The experience of the Alberta-Canada All Breeds Association operating out of the Calgary airport is that the bids for proposed contracts for flights out of the Calgary airport by Air Canada were one third higher than those coming from United States carriers for the same job.
These bids were based on Air Canada's using a standard DC-8 with a capacity of 65,000 pounds. I want to report that Air Canada did move about 11 loads with this type of equipment during the month of December out of the Toronto airport. These were mostly lighter weight dairy cattle that were going to the Mediterranean. The reason Air Canada is not competitive with foreign carriers is that while Air Canada's cost per pound may be competitive with other carriers, its cost per head is far from competitive. I suppose the principal reason is that Air Canada's competitors are using larger aircraft which are able to take bigger pay loads. The cost per head can be reduced significantly by using that approach.
However, much more important than being competitive, Air Canada continues to insist on its right of first refusal on all proposed contracts for airlifting of Canadian cattle out of Canadian airports. The only comment which I think is appropriate is that surely this is a dog-in-the-manger attitude which does not help two air forwarders, or more for that matter, who may wish to organize in Canada and to get into what appears to be the very good business of exporting Canada's excellent breeding cattle to a world-wide market.
I suggest that there are some very direct consequences of this right of first refusal upon which Air Canada insists. This information again comes from these two forwarders. World Wide Forwarders is one of the largest and most progressive forwarders in North America, and perhaps in the world. As a result of this policy World Wide has had to acquire its own aircraft. It cannot use its own aircraft out of Canadian airports for the reasons I have cited, so World Wide trucks Canadian cattle it acquires for offshore customers to the United States and then uses its own aircraft and quite a number of other foreign aircraft to complete the job and to forward to customers abroad.
Air Canada
The Alberta-Canada All Breeds Association which operates out of Calgary is presently trucking its cattle from various locations in Alberta, and perhaps from other parts of Western Canada, to Montana. Most of the shipments go to Great Falls, Montana, where they are loaded onto foreign carriers. This group has a contract for about one airload per week for a full year, and possibly considerably more at the completion of that undertaking. All of these types of contracts for airlifting cattle are for foreign customers, and all of them are across at least one ocean. The only practical way to move the cattle is by aircraft.
Both Canadian forwarders are mindful of some of Air Canada's special problems which have developed as a result of limited experience. One of them is a problem regarding ventilation of aircraft when flying livestock. Just shortly before Christmas about half a load-several hundred cattle

died as a result of poor ventilation on one of the trips about which I have been speaking. I suggest that that was the result of lack of experience. It is a poor way to build confidence and to attract Canadian customers. Air Canada has limited experience and not much desire to get into the air freighting of livestock.
Both these truly Canadian forwarders are knowledgeable about the worldwide popularity of and demand for our dairy and beef cattle, and are trying to fit that into their business of forwarding breeding cattle to customers all over the world. This country has built a good reputation for both breeding and dairy cattle over the years, in part because of the high standards imposed by the health of animals branch. Both these forwarders would like to see an air freight carrier-a Boeing 707 or similar wide-bodied aircraft-make weekly shipments of live cattle to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. They have enough firm orders for several years, but in order to ship once a week out of Calgary, Edmonton and more often from Montreal, they would have to insist on a more efficient walk-on system than Air Canada uses at the present time. If Air Canada is not prepared to supply such a facility then I suggest that foreign carriers be allowed to offer it at Canadian airports.
1 am sure the president of Air Canada, Mr. Claude Taylor, is well aware of these representations as he has received correspondence from both these forwarders and from other Canadian cattle organizations about the situation. His letters, which appear in the flight magazine En Route, indicate his interest in matters relating to the airline. He must be aware of the potential for Canada's balance of trade position through air freighting cattle, since every animal transported goes to an export market. This is a relatively new market which is waiting, even begging, for good Canadian cattle.
In the past few years our cattle industry has been depressed, but this new concept has helped attract foreign customers. The market is there, the price is right, and Air Canada has an obligation to help move the cattle. I suggest that a realistic air

freight policy could enhance our total balance of payments picture considerably.
1 have no problem with the Senate amendments to this bill for the reorganization of Air Canada, Mr. Speaker. I think we will have a better organized and better administered national airline as a result of them. I wish to commend the Senate for becoming involved and bringing something of this nature to this House for ratification, and I fully support the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to add to the comments of my colleagues on the bill respecting the reorganization of Air Canada. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) brought up an excellent point. Farm income in western Canada has decreased rapidly over the last three years. Many farmers and ranchers have spent years acquiring expertise in the breeding of cattle, hogs, and other livestock, and it seems unfair that we cannot provide the kind of aircraft necessary for this livestock to be exported. This is a business which would help increase prairie farm income.
It is ironic that, as we debate the Senate amendments to the bill to reorganize Air Canada, the government has just approved a new budget for the airlines. The press release I have here indicates that Air Canada's 1978 capital budget for the purchase of new aircraft will be in the neighbourhood of $68.5 million. The capitalization of the airline is not very high and that is why we are now considering amendments to the act-to enable Air Canada to be free of the hold of the CNR and go forward as a Crown corporation. The financial reorganization bill before us reduces Air Canada's debt to equity ratio from the current 95 to 5 to 60 to 40, which is a more traditional situation for North American air carriers. The equity will increase from the current $5 million now held by CNR to $340 million, all held by the Crown corporation, Air Canada.
Some of the amendments proposed and argued by hon. members in the other place were debated very effectively on this side of the House before the bill went to the other place. In particular I should like to refer to the deletion of clause 6(2) which reads as follows:
The Governor in Council may, by order, authorize the Corporation to engage in or carry on any activities not otherwise authorized by this Act.
