subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
that Bill C-229, to protect the Canadian environment by instituting mandatory impact assessment procedures prior to the con-
January 31, 1978

struction of installations potentially damaging to the environment, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in an age of supposed rational enlightenment, it is unfortunate that our society still seems able to respond only to crisis demand situations. Yet how many in this room today can remember having heard the word pollution more than 15 years ago, let alone having been actively involved in the alarm that was raised in our society at that time?
I recall being elected to the British Columbia legislature in 1966 without the issue ever being raised in the campaign, let alone on the floor of the House by either the government or the opposition in the ensuing year. However, by 1968-69 the small vocal group of seemingly radical doomsday soothsayers had grown into a large public outcry, leading to public and political pressure and the subsequent beginnings of the legislative process.
By the early seventies a considerable and credible body of scientific and professional environmentalists emerged and gained credibility as well as bureaucratic positioning within governments. Within a decade, society had moved from the more negative expressionism of pollution and severe attack on the great villains, government and industry, and evolved into the more moderate expressions of the word environment and broadening the general perspective, to recognizing that all human activity encroaches on the natural environment, to a recognition of the limits of growth, and to a condemnation of the developed world by the developing nations for its gluttonous consumption, and finally to the concept of a conservation ethic and awareness that big is bad and that we need a reassessment of our entire value system and life style.
Often a recurring trend in film art provides us with a mirror of our current cultural or ethical values. I saw a movie a short time ago that reflected and simplified one such current value. The movie was called "Oh God". The story centred around a young man working in a grocery store who claimed to have heard and seen God, who had asked him to bring the message of the hour to man from God, the basic message being God gave us the world for us to live in and He provided all that we need; all we had to do was make it work. The choice is ours individually and if we so choose it will work well for us, but if we choose to destroy His creations the inevitable doomsday would be upon us. A movie such as this in both form and substance would have been laughed at and mocked out of existence less than a decade ago among the symbols of "Easy Rider" and "Clockwork Orange".
Today, whether it is "Rocky" or "Star Wars" or "Oh God", people are reaching out to the message of that movie because a new generation has been born, educated, and has accepted a new or renewed ethic of conservation. The ethic of pessimism, wanton desecration, and fantasy has passed and a new generation has emerged speaking, believing, and feeling the need to balance and harmonize productivity and consumption with conservation and replenishment.
Environment
This House and this government, as well as the next House and the next government, may well not recognize that before us is in fact an extension of those new or renewed basic values or ethics. Before the next decade has passed this and other legislation based upon these ethics or values will be in place. Consequently any delaying tactics to prevent its passage or broaden its discussion will only be temporary because this piece of legislation in its principles is in tune with its time, it is right morally, and ethically right according to the values of the next generation, if not this generation.
This current generation of legislators has responded to the call of a few radicals and visionaries in an effort to pacify rather than to create from an inner environmental value and conviction, and for this reason, under the pressure of energy demands, unemployment and inflation, the environmental cause may be unfortunately forced to rest a while, but be assured this force will come again with a new inner conviction.
I urge Canadians listening today to give this legislation a chance. Listen to this legislation. Open it for further discussion in order that these basic principles will be recognized by legislators tomorrow as they are being recognized by the legislators today.
We have in the last decade advanced rapidly and progressively. Through this period of rapid growth of environmental technology standards and legislation, while some programs have applied technology successfully, it is time to assess our future direction in restoring and maintaining a harmonious environment.
On the negative side, environmental concerns have been paralleled by decreasing productivity and deterioration of the work ethic. Energy and inflation crises have successfully challenged environmental priorities. The individual has no status in law to come into court and challenge a project unless it is going to damage his own person or his own property. Most legislation created by governments tends to be after-the-fact legislation, and at the federal level the Fisheries Act still remains the only effective veto relative to developmental projects.
On the more positive side, environmental concerns are firmly entrenched in both the public and the private sector, and while legislation remains largely toothless, it does enunciate wordy principles and has resulted in a firmly entrenched professional bureaucracy.
How many times does one hear citizens declaring that it is useless to protest or to take action because the government or other institutions will not listen; an indication of apathy? Toffler's book "Future Shock" supports the theory that the individual whose role in society has become increasingly insignificant, whose sphere of personal action has been reduced, perceives most of social reality as being beyond personal control.
Decentralization of organization must take place. There must emerge a form of redistribution of power to individuals and communities. Today most things are done through organizations, but human beings are in these organizations. They
January 31, 1978

Environment
can, and they must insist that organizations are meant to serve men, not men to serve organizations.
To ensure that there is active public participation, one is in need of two elements. There must exist a legal basis for participation and there must be mechanisms for public involvement. If one studies the various pieces of federal environmental legislation in Canada, such as the federal government's Clean Air Act, and Water Act, one realizes that citizens are not guaranteed the right to participate in public and private decisions concerning resource development and management. The Canadian legal system does not guarantee or even promise those rights.
The convening of public hearings, such as the Berger Commission, is a discretionary power given to an official, not a requirement. Only the federal government's Northern Inland Waters Act manifests any commitment to participation by the public in making of environmental management decisions.
Section 26 of the Canada Water Act (1970) states that the minister may establish advisory committees if he considers them desirable. Ele may appoint to these committees such persons as he desires, and he is under no obligation to be in any way influenced by the advice given to him by the committees. The Clean Air Act does not contemplate any compulsory citizen participation in the making of any environmental quality decisions. There is a provision in the National Energy Board Act for the holding of public hearings, but the statute does not define what procedure is to be followed. The Board may determine its own procedure.
After the release of the Environment Canada report on ecological consequences of the James Bay hydro dam system, the federal government publicized a new administrative program called EARP. The Minister of the Environment, at his discretion, could call for an environmental impact assessment prior to the construction of a federal project. This policy mechanism is a false front. The government can talk about its commitment to the protection of the environment. However, it never has to put that commitment to work.
If a political party holds a majority, a minister is not bound to act on regulations which do not have the clout of statute. As usual, it is the individual without political or economic power who loses. My bill would bring the decision-making process out of the smoke-filled back rooms and into the open. The individual citizen's rights would be guaranteed.
The ineffectiveness of the existing regulations is compounded by what governments have chosen to leave out. They ask only for a narrowly defined environmental study, whereas in my bill the environment includes the human population. Another problem of definition exists because the term "projects" is used in the regulations. Undertakings other than projects, such as policies or legislative proposals, are therefore not included, and when a policy proposal has achieved the "project" stage it means the cabinet has already given the green light, so the assessment procedure becomes an exercise or a detailing of consequences. Not only that, it is a gross

waste of public money and constitutes an added cost which should never be incurred. Environmental assessments which are not carried out before decisions are made are, in effect, valueless, nothing but sand in the gears.
Of graver concern is the complete lack of an opportunity for the public to contribute to the decision-making process. The minister may sit in his office, read the proponent's report, approve it, and the next minute the concrete starts to flow.
There is a substantial discretionary power in the hands of the proponent of a project. A federal agency or department, or a private company operating on a federal grant, has the discretion itself to decide that its proposal will have practically no environmental impact. If the proponent makes that decision, and if it sticks, he can go ahead without being subject to the impact assessment procedures. Again, if he can satisfy the screening committee that the environmental impact will only be minor, he can also go ahead without assessment. And even if the assessment procedure applies, it is the proponent, not the department, not an outside agency, which prepares the initial assessment. The environmental assessment panel sets down guidelines, but the proponent himself determines how those guidelines apply to the initial assessment.
The "front program" which the government has supposedly adopted and which will supposedly assure that no program will go ahead in the absence of an environmental assessment, has now proven to be ineffective. The fact is that such projects do go ahead without assessment. This is made possible because of the discretionary powers left with ministers. Each year more than 1,000 projects are screened for potential adverse environmental effects. Time has shown that on the average only five per year are deemed to have significant environmental effects, qualifying them for an initial study.
The powers of the assessment panel are limited. For one thing, it has the capacity only to review impact assessments prepared by the proponent. Then, if it does find fault, it has only the power to advise, and it can be ignored or overruled by the minister or by the cabinet.
In the case of multi-phase projects, it appears to be the practice of the Department of the Environment to conduct environmental impact assessments one stage at a time. In practice this means that if the first phase of a multi-phase project can be cleared environmentally the whole thing will go ahead, because a proponent will argue that so much has been invested in the development of the first stage that the investment commitment should outweigh any adverse environmental factors which appear later on. That seems to be the approach the Department of the Environment is taking to projects at both Wreck Cove in Nova Scotia, and in northwestern British Columbia, in the minister's own riding.
Bill C-229 would ensure that undertakings in which the federal government has any type of interest are planned with due consideration for the environment. My bill has several key provisions which fill gaps in existing federal environmental legislation and administrative processes. They are as follows:
January 31, 1978

1.	Any undertaking by the Government of Canada, or under its legislative authority or funded by it in any manner, must submit an impact assessment to the Minister of the Environment. This is not spelled out clearly in existing legislation.
2.	All persons should have access to the impact assessment. At the present time information is withheld, or can be withheld; the public is not allowed access to scientific information connected with impact assessment.
3.	A public hearing at which any person may participate must be held before the minister makes a decision. At the present time there is no provision that any such hearing must take place. Decisions can be made and projects completed in the absence of any public participation or any public hearing.
4.	Funds provided by the proponent should be made available at the minister's discretion to responsible participants acting in the public interest. This would assist in ensuring full, intelligent, and competent discussion. As things are, many people are in a position to see that something is being done which is wrong. They feel it is wrong, but they lack the confidence or the information which would enable them to prove their case. Information should be provided by the government or by the proponents of the plan to be used by those who contend that the project should not proceed and need this information to prove their point.
I am concerned that environmental legislation is presently being used only as "sand-in-the-gears" whose result is to slow projects down or to make them more expensive. Very often responsibility for taking environmental decisions is passed from one minister to another, and in the end nobody makes a decision. As I say, it is merely sand in the gears. That is not the case with my bill; the minister could make such a provision. Provision is also made for class actions. Any person could appeal the minister's decision in court.
The concept behind environmental impact assessment is rooted in the moral obligation to accept the interdependence of the earth's ecosystem, and act accordingly. Man must junk his faith in his own dominance to the trash can of narrowly conceived ideas. Everything and anything can only take so much kicking around. The vulnerability of man stems from his pressure upon and manipulation of the environment. Technology will not be able to fabricate substitutes which yield the same satisfaction for natural habitat resources which man has exploited to the point of non-productibility or irreversibility.
If we examine our material progress to date, the inescapable fact is that the largest part has come from the conversion of our natural resources into-

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. What then could be more logical than a legislative mechanism which helps to safeguard the rights of individuals who derive some form of wealth from the services of our natural resources?
In the recently introduced nuclear control bill provision is made for public hearings-a reaction to public protestations of nuclear facilities being put up in their backyard without public debate. Not very much is spelled out in the legislation as to how public hearings are to be conducted, but at least there is provision for them. At least there is some minor sign that the government remains open, although largely ignorant of the real requirements of an environmental impact assessment.
There is some minimal amount of radiation associated with a uranium mine, nuclear reactor, or a coal-fired electrical generation plant. Apparently the number of premature deaths caused by the entire coal fuel cycle is much higher than that considered as possible for a uranium fuel cycle.
If the federal government decides to help develop coal generated electricity, are those people potentially affected by, say, coal ash, to be treated in a different manner than those potential victims of the uranium fuel cycle's radiation? I think not. Both groups should have the opportunity to participate in a public hearing, a right my legislation would give them.
Public hearings are not perfect policy-making devices, and we all know that because we have attended or participated in them many times as politicians. What results from a public hearing is a variety of different, often self-interested views, some facts about and perhaps some novel untested solutions to a problem. But public hearings do perform several useful functions; gathering information, increasing public participation and acceptability of decisions, and assisting decision-makers, the minister and his civil servants, to choose from different alternatives that may be put forward.
Why is the government so afraid of information? Why is it so afraid of facts? If that is all this legislation does, it could produce information to improve a decision and to make sure a decision is morally right.
Legislation of the sort I have proposed requires comprehensive freedom of information laws. Without access to government research documents, the public's hands are tied. An excellent example is the attempt, which I brought up recently in the national resources standing committee, of citizens trying to prepare good briefs respecting the nuclear waste issue without access to many government documents which are now classified confidential. These 30 environmental groups from across Canada were notified only two weeks ahead that they could appear and present a brief before the committee. They are told that they cannot have the information that is available to the committee, the same scientific government information-"make your brief but get your own material." Why, if this is public information, is it not available to all the people making objections? It seems almost ridiculous to believe that government in this day and age would withhold such information.
80031 -t

January 31, 1978
Environment
I do not want this legislation to be used to stall worthy projects solely because some minuscule faction deems it unworthy. In Bill C-229 I have tried to ensure that an efficient and fair examination be given to all federal government undertakings which have been deemed to affect the environment in some manner. I am more than willing to listen to any group or individual who has ideas on how to speed up the process while still attaining the legislation's objectives.
Bill C-229 would not bloat the bureaucracy, because the civil servants who administer the existing environmental assessment review would instead carry out the provisions of my bill. Several provinces, Australia, many United States states, and the U.S. federal government have legislation that requires government departments within their jurisdiction to go through some sort of environmental assessment review process. I have taken the best from their legislation, discarded the worst, and added some of my own ideas. I believe strongly that if not the bill then the subject matter should be passed on to the committee stage.
I have dozens of letters of support for my bill. Many groups, ranging from oil companies to environmental organizations, want to appear before the standing committee to discuss environmental impact assessments. They want to appear because this subject is timely. Has this government its ear to hear? The government would have a chance to defend its new EARP program and to find out if it is lacking, where it might act and where it might change. I think it would be an objective kind of committee, that it would be open to new ideas, to the flow of new information. The government has nothing to fear, it has only to gain and to learn.
If at least the subject matter of Bill C-229 were sent to committee, we could get going on this issue now and not before it is too late.
Courage is often associated with standing firm against opposition. Such courage is as important today as ever. But perhaps more important today is the courage to move, to innovate, to make decisions. In the emerging society of today, the decisions are becoming much more complex. Decisions call for inventiveness as well as firmness. Only by combining sensitivity to human needs with rigorous understanding of social processes can we make sound decisions. Decisions of the future must be worked out by men and women at their jobs in a world of specialized functions.
The major decisions of our time concern far-ranging issues of the use of power, the relation of men to machines, the relation of men to environment, the establishing of freedom in an increasingly organized world. These decisions must be made by men such as ourselves, gathered here today, men who exercise power and live day in and day out in the midst of their responsibilities.
We need criticism and help from those who see issues from varied perspectives. We need the advice of scientists. But, most important of all we need the wisdom and the participation of people as well as the insight of specialists. All people share the risks of our decisions and all people have a right to participate in the shaping of those decisions.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh A. Anderson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, protection of the Canadian environment is an issue that concerns all Canadians, and I welcome the hon. member's proposal as another expression of that concern. As you know, the government has already taken positive steps to meet this issue through the formation of the Department of the Environment, and the establishment of an environmental assessment and review process through a cabinet decision in December, 1973.
The process covers activities and projects initiated by federal departments and agencies and those involving federal funds or property. Federal departments must examine their planned proposals and refer those with potentially significant environmental effects to the environmental assessment panel in the Department of the Environment for review. The panel sets guidelines for the preparation of an environmental impact statement by the project proponent, and releases this statement for public evaluation. After reviewing the environmental impact statement and obtaining the views of the public through hearings, the panel recommends appropriate action to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) based on the environmental consequences involved. The decision to implement the panel's recommendations is made by the Minister of the Environment and his colleagues whose departments are initiating or sponsoring the proposals.
There are now 21 such projects under review, and these include the gas pipeline from the Arctic to southern Canada proposed by Polar Gas, the extension to the Vancouver International Airport by the Department of Transport, and the development of uranium refineries in Saskatchewan and Ontario by Eldorado Nuclear Limited. We can all appreciate the complexities involved in projects of this size and nature, as well as the length of time required to produce a meaningful environmental assessment.
Our present assessment process is a very flexible instrument which can be adjusted easily to accommodated required changes. Based on present experience with the assessment process, changes are being considered now which will broaden the capabilities of the environmental assessment panel to review projects that are referred by federal departments and agencies. We plan to keep the assessment process under continuing review to determine further adjustments or changes which may be needed to make it as effective as possible.
Unfortunately, Bill C-229 does not improve the government's ability to assess the environmental consequences of projects for which it is responsible. The bill proposes to give federal courts an appellate decision-making power on the merits of a proposed action. In this connection, I should like to refer to the following provisions which relate to environmental assessment decisions made by the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc). Clause 19 of the bill reads as follows:
Any person may, within 10 days of the minister's decision, apply to the Federal Court for a review of that decision.
January 31, 1978

Clause 20 of the bill reads as follows:
The Federal Court shall determine the matter de novo, and may examine the environmental impact assessment, the review, any submission made to the minister and such further material as is necessary in the opinion of the court to reach a decision.
Clause 22. (1) reads as follows:
The Federal Court shall determine the matters in question within a reasonable period of time after Final day of the hearing.
Traditionally our courts have intervened to set aside administrative decision where the procedure required by law has not been followed or where an administrative decision is shown, on the basis of the evidence adduced, to be plainly arbitrary or capricious. But it has never been the practice of our courts, nor do our judges have special competence, to substitute their value judgments for those of others. To require our courts to undertake such a responsibility would be inconsistent with our system of democratic government and would be an inappropriate use of the judiciary.
The author of Bill C-229 does not appear to have considered carefully how a federal environmental impact assessment act will fit with existing statutory responsibilities such as, for example, the responsibilities of certain regulatory bodies to take account of environmental concerns. Is it intended to repeal the statutory responsibility of the Yukon and Northwest Territories water boards which were established under the Northern Inland Waters Act? Those boards were established to provide, pursuant to section 9 of the act, the following:
- the conservation, development and utilization of the water resources of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories in a manner that will provide the optimum benefit therefrom for all Canadians and for the residents of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories in particular.
Is it intended to remove from the National Energy Board its perceived statutory responsibility under section 44 of the National Energy Board Act to take account of environmental concerns in deciding whether to issue a certificate of public convenience and necessity for the construction of interprovincial pipelines, which is a perceived statutory responsibility that has caused the board to require applicants for such certificate to undertake environmental impact assessments?
These examples illustrate the need to consider carefully how the requirements of a federal environmental impact assessment act should dovetail with existing statutory responsibilities, both federal and provincial, which require regulatory bodies to satisfy themselves regarding environmental matters. I am sure all hon. members would agree that needless duplication of time and money should be avoided.
Many of the provisions of Bill C-229 have been borrowed from existing legislation, such as the United States national environmental policy act and the environmental assessment act, 1975, of Ontario. These provisions were tossed into the pot, as it were, without due consideration having been given to the purpose and scheme of the acts from which they were borrowed. The decision-making power Bill C-299 would propose to give the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment has been evidently borrowed from the environmental assessment act, 1975, of Ontario. However, it should be noted that the
Environment
word "undertaking" in the Ontario act is much narrower in scope than the scope given to the word in Bill C-229. The Ontario act defines "undertaking" as an "enterprise or activity." At present it applies only to enterprises, activities or projects by or on behalf of the government of Ontario, and by public bodies or municipalities. The proclamation of the Lieutenant Governor required by section 3(b) of the act, making the act applicable to any major commercial or business enterprise or activity designated by the regulations-for example, projects by the private sector-has not yet been made. For that matter, neither have the regulations.
The definition proposed in section 2(d) of Bill C-229 for environmental impact assessment is taken, with the substitution of the word "undertaking" for the word "action", from section 102(2)C of the United States national environmental policy act. However, this definition is preceded in the NEPA document by the following statement:
The Congress authorizes and directs that, to the fullest extent possible-
(2) all agencies of the federal government shall

(c) include in every recommendation or report on proposals for legislation and other major federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment a detailed statement by the responsible official-
As will be apparent when considered in context, the five point enumeration in NEPA is not intended to define what an environmental impact assessment statement should contain. The contents of any environmental impact statement ought to be based on what is being assessed and not on some abstract definition of what should be contained in the statement in which the assessment is written up. The United States council of environmental quality, CEQ, which was established by NEPA, has published extensive guidelines designed to assist federal agencies in preparing environmental impact statements. The latest was issued in 1975.
In conclusion, Bill C-229 will not produce an effective and efficient environmental assessment procedure. It does not improve in any way the government's existing capability in this area which is provided by the environmental assessment and review process.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see that the opposition is very anxious about this bill and that it would like the House to proceed immediately to a vote. As chairman of the committee on fisheries and forestry, which has jurisdiction over environmental matters, I am surprised to see how anxious the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) is for this bill to be put to a vote when-perhaps 1 should not say so here-sometimes we need several sittings of the committee to pass certain bills.
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate my colleague for Fraser Valley West because, as I have just said, he is a member of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and is greatly concerned with the environment. It could perhaps be said that, as all members of the committee are aware, he shows a certain obstinacy about this problem which greatly
80031-1 t V2

January 31, 1978
Environment
concerns him, as it concerns of course every member of the House and every Canadian. The environment in which we are all condemned to live on this earth-as I see the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard), I would even say in this valley of sorrows-the protection of this environment is a daily concern for all Canadians and especially the federal government, and Bill C-229 submitted for our consideration by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West expresses once again this concern, not only of the representatives of the people, but also of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, as you and all members of the House who insist on being kept well informed are aware, the present government has made positive efforts to meet the concerns of Canadians expressed by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West in Bill C-229, first by creating the Department of Environment, and they by establishing in December 1973 an environmental assessment and review process. I believe that the French word "environnemental" is rather modern and that it was not accepted before 1960. This word was not used at that time, but it is now accepted by the Academie canadienne-fran$aise and the Academie franchise.
From the very beginning, Environment Canada has endeavoured to measure the level of pollution caused by the federal government. It also assesses the projects in which it participates financially in one way or another so that these projects will comply with the guidelines aimed at eliminating or restricting contamination of the environment.
In 1972, the cabinet approved a recommendation from a ministerial committee to the effect that the environmental impact of any new project of the federal government should be scrutinized. It is precisely in light of that policy of the Canadian government that Friday last week I asked the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a question concerning an issue of considerable interest for us in Magdalen Islands, that is the possible effects of the development of salt deposits discovered there.
In fact, if the present government of the province of Quebec does not delay the project, the salt mine discovered in Magdalen Islands should become productive by the end of 1978. Being ever optimistic I would say to my friend the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. LaSalle) that to haul that salt away we shall necessarily have to build harbour facilities as those deposits are located on an island. The project of the provincial government involving the financial participation of the federal government implies the building of a deep water wharf on a site which fishermen and municipal authorities consider detrimental to fish and particularly lobster stocks.
As we know, lobster fishing is the main source of income for Magdalen Islands fishermen and residents. We should be very careful and study seriously the concerns expressed by Fishermen. Since the federal government will contribute financially to the project it wonders if in view of that policy and that process it should not initiate an environmental study in this area. I am told that, according to provincial experts, there is

no risk for lobster stocks but fishermen who are sceptical by nature do not readily believe this assertion of the so-called experts from the provincial environment department.
Pollution is not our only source of environmental concern, Mr. Speaker, although more importance seems to be given to air and water pollution. It is not the only sphere of federal action in this matter. There are a number of other factors which must be taken into consideration. Among other things, the damaging effect of physical obstacles on the water community and the migratory paths of various wildlife, as well as the irresponsible development of non renewable resources, including land.
Thus on December 20, 1973 a cabinet decision instituted the environmental assessment and review process so that, first, the environmental factor would be taken into consideration at the planning stage of new federal projects, programs or activities, all the while respecting provincial jurisdictions, and second, so as to submit all potentially hazardous projects to an environmental assessment prior to irrevocable commitments or decisions. Third, to take into account the results of such an assessment in the planning, decision making and implementation process.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, despite the importance of Bill C-229 introduced by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman), that the steps taken so far by the government of Canada meet the concerns he expresses in his bill. Earlier he criticized the Clean Air Act and other statutes, saying they are not mandatory. But I am surprised to see that a Progressive Conservative like the hon. member for Fraser Valley West in particular should always want to impose some restriction such as that on the freedom of the people in Canada. I do not criticize his position on the protection of our environment but the way he wants to stop everything by mandatory and coercive measures, if I may put it that way. And that is characteristic of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, as I said earlier. He will not let go. I indicated at the beginning of my remarks what his attitude was in this area at the meetings of the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, which also includes environment. As my colleague the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. Anderson) pointed out earlier in his enthusiasm to support the cause he has always felt strongly about, I believe this bill derives from certain pieces of legislation already in existence in Ontario and to the south but he arranged them to suit his purpose and I believe that is why we have here a provision that could run counter to certain customs in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that today everybody is concerned with the quality of life, and Canadian society, as all societies facing this problem, is wondering what decisions should be made. I think that survival is also included in quality of life, and I believe that people must have the means to survive and earn their living. For some fifteen years pollution and all those things resembling pollution have rightly been the subject of considerable concern. We keep hearing today about the environmental impact which might ensue from given projects
January 31, 1978

scheduled for certain areas in need of regional or industrial development.
What are governments doing about that problem? They are going to do what they have done till today and what the hon. member for Fraser Valley West suggests, but at what expense? At the expense of not only money but time and many speeches. During that time there are projects, for example in a non-polluted area such as ours-I am talking about the Gaspe area and a good part of the province of Quebec not located in the surroundings of Canada's metropolis-there are projects that could have been born in a very short delay but which are being postponed because of unnecessary complications imposed by certain statutes because of the effects on the environment.
Which is more important: to see to it that our citizens are fed or to set aside development projects which could help them feed themselves while bringing them the ideal quality of life environmentalists hope for? I can understand that the problem is a difficult one to solve for the governments, I understand its importance and I do not want to criticize those who-

It may be that we have not done enough, that we did not utter that word "environment" early enough, that we did not concern ourselves with it. subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1977 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when private members' hour began I was discussing the deletion of clause 6(2) of the bill which reads as follows:
The Governor in Council may, by order, authorize the Corporation to engage in or carry on any activities not otherwise authorized by this Act.
The deletion of this clause is a welcome move as it granted undue power to the governor in council to enlarge the scope or completely change the nature of the activities carried on by Air Canada without coming back to parliament for authority. This is a dangerous precedent and if the clause were enacted it could weaken parliamentary power. In addition, Senator Gro-sart pointed out in the deliberations in the other place that this clause contravenes the government's basic guidelines for crown corporations. The Privy Council office document entitled

January 31, 1978
Air Canada
"Crown Corporations, Direction, Control, Accountability- Government of Canada Proposals 1977", states:
It is commonly understood that crown corporations, although largely independent of parliamentary scrutiny and controls, are still in the final analysis instruments of parliament. Logic then dictates that parliament should exercise what might be called the shareholder's prerogative with respect to crown corporations on behalf of the Canadian public.
The message contained in this policy statement is clearly that as long as a corporation is a Crown corporation, its authority for action rests with parliament. By removing the necessity of dealing with parliament, this clause may well provide Air Canada with a certain amount of added flexibility. However, as long as Air Canada remains a Crown corporation, its flexibility must of necessity be restricted.
The controversy over this one clause highlights the conflict of ideas concerning what should be the limits and bounds of a Crown corporation. Passage of Bill C-3, in its present form, could serve to cloud further the distinction between Crown corporations and private corporations. One of the major provisions of Bill C-3 grants to Air Canada the power to embark on auxiliary projects, other than air transportation, such as the management of hotels and travel agencies and perhaps even extending to trucking. In April of 1974, I rose in the House to speak on a similar bill dealing with financial arrangements for the CNR and argued that the CNR had no mandate to become embroiled in the hotel and real estate businesses.
I would like to restate my thinking in a nutshell. A crown corporation should not become involved in areas where private enterprise has the willingness and the wherewithal to provide the service or the product. In the Canadian context, private firms have almost invariably provided a better service and done a better job of running business than government.
Given the exemplary record of CNR with regard to hotel management, allowing Air Canada to get into this business gives me room for great concern. The original mandate of Air Canada as a Crown corporation was to provide safe and efficient air service both within and outside this country. The business of Air Canada was seen to be the air business. It is my strong belief that the original mandate of this corporation should be strictly adhered to.
During the debate this past fall on Bill C-3, many members from the Edmonton area raised the question of the difficulties which lie with the Edmonton international airport. By virtue of clause 6(1 )(b) and (c), the government will allow the airlines to build facilities to help in their operations. My contention is that the government should allow the airlines more freedom in discussing what type of terminals they will generally have to service the public. If they were given that opportunity, I think you would see much less in the way of grandiose structures such as Mirabel and Calgary and perhaps a great deal more efficient structures wherein the landing fees, and so on, would not be so expensive for the airlines.
I wish to mention two areas of concern to me and perhaps suggest to the minister how he can follow this up. The first is

the problem of preclearance at Edmonton International Airport. Calgary and Edmonton were both to get preclearance at about the same time. The problem is that the facilities at Edmonton International Airport are incapable of handling this at this time. Budgetary restraints mean that more money cannot be provided at the present time.
I suggest to the minister that in order to provide these facilities in time for the Commonwealth Games this summer he attempt to negotiate with the United States air carriers to see if they will provide preclearance personnel to Edmonton on the basis of cheap, temporary facilities being set up now with the promise that, as soon as budgetary restraints allow the building of permanent facilities, these will be put in place. I feel they may look at that type of suggestion, particularly if we say it will be within one or two years of the time of the promise.
The other problem is customs clearance after arrival at the airport. I want briefly to state what happened to one of my constituents. I will not get too deeply into this because my colleagues from Edmonton have already stated this problem bluntly and seriously. I quote from a letter that I recently received:
My wife and I recently had the unfortunate experience of having to clear Canadian customs at the Edmonton international airport. I say unfortunate because there were approximately 440 other people on our flight also trying to clear. We were all forced up one escalator into a room that was overflowing with people and only the quick action of a fellow passenger, in turning off the escalator, averted what could have been a serious accident with people unable to get off the moving stairs because of the full room.
Ministry of Transport officials in Edmonton state that this facility for customs preclearance was designed for a Vanguard capable of carrying about 90 passengers. Today arriving at that terminal are 747s carrying over 400 people. It can be seen that even with the $400,000 allowed to expand this facility temporarily, the problem still exists. There is a great need for something to be done very quickly to alleviate this problem.
One amendment to clause 6(2) restricts the ability of Air Canada to go beyond subclauses (a), (b), (c) and (d) so far as what they can do in the way of expansion without coming to government. Herein lies the problem of Air Canada's intended purchase of Nordair. Before such a purchase can be made and because of amendments to the act, they should come before a parliamentary committee in order that it can deal with the reasons why Air Canada would like to get into the regional air carrier business.
Throughout the history of regional air carriers in Canada there has been a problem. From their earliest beginnings as bush pilot operations, these airlines have typified for many the spirit of adventure that has made our country what it is today. Nordair has been no exception. In 1968, 21 years after the beginnings of Nordair, it was the first airline to land a jet aircraft in the Northwest Territories.
The policy statement of regional airlines set forth by the Minister of Transport in 1966 outlined the role which regional airlines would be permitted to play in the near future. The regionals were to provide regular route operations into the
January 31, 1978

north and operate local and regional routes to complement the main carriers. It was a distinct policy which was somewhat refined in 1969 by the designation of definite geographic areas in each region.
Air Canada's intended purchase of Nordair is a concern for me. It means the elimination of a small but very efficient regional air carrier, a competitor, and the intrusion of a strictly mainline air carrier into the regional business.
Nordair has provided excellent service to the public of eastern Ontario and northwestern Quebec. It has fulfilled a quite separate function from that being fulfilled by Air Canada. My worry is that the Air Canada takeover may weaken the traditional commitment of Nordair to its travelling public. It may lead to an unfortunate abandonment of low profit routes.
I have put forward a number of my concerns about the Air Canada bill. I do not intend to outline those concerns that have already been covered by my colleagues. I just want to make one last comment regarding the profitability of Air Canada.
It concerns me somewhat that the management of Air Canada would provide air passes to their employees on other than a standby basis. If we want to reward our employees for productivity, that is a good thing to do. Obviously the productivity of Air Canada has increased in the last year. Their profits show that. However, providing employees with passes would average about $300 per person; if they are provided also to wives or husbands or relatives, the number could go as high as 40,000. That would almost eat up the total profit this airline accumulated in the past year.
Something else that bothers me is there is no stipulation that the pass must be used in Canada. The deficit in the tourist industry in this country in 1971 was $202 million. It is calculated to be $1.3 billion today. We must take a careful look at the decisions made by the Corporation.
We are glad to see in the bill a clause providing that Air Canada's report must be brought before the transport committee each year. After all, we do represent the shareholders, and Crown corporations are still responsible to the parliament of Canada. May I add that I am pleased that the other place saw fit to make these amendments; we in this party thought they were very necessary at the time we were discussing second reading.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1977 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, have a few brief comments to make on Bill C-3. I note the measure authorizes Air Canada to engage in a wider range of activities having to do, for example, with hotels and travel agencies. I commend our caucus critic, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), on the important role he played in the discussion of this legislation. At the committee level he proposed many amendments, and a good many of the amendments put forward by my party were accepted. The bill has been returned to the House from the Senate because one
Air Canada
amendment which we proposed was not accepted by the House of Commons.
Among the positive proposals made by the Conservative party in the committee was that the annual report of Air Canada be referred to a standing committee on an annual basis. In this connection it is noteworthy that the corporation's annual report has not been before a committee since November, 1973. Also, we would have enshrined in legislation a provision that Air Canada should have due regard to sound business principles and, in particular, to the contemplation of profit. Mr. Pratte, the former chairman of Air Canada, always complained that he did not really know what the purpose of the corporation was.
We on this side are glad the Senate saw fit to eliminate clause 6(2) from the legislation and that the minister has seen fit to support this recommendation. I will put the pertinent part of the clause on record. It stated that the governor-incouncil "may by order authorize the corporation to engage in or carry on activities not otherwise authorized by this act." It is obvious that undue powers would have been given to the cabinet or to the governor in council. We in this party have always believed in parliamentary control.
While this legislation was before the Senate it is interesting to note that the secretary of Air Canada had this to say about clause 6(2):
The wording and the concept was not suggested by Air Canada; it was proposed by the government itself in the original drafting as a means of avoiding having to go back to parliament to clarify a point which was really something which could be handled administratively in the context of the broad powers given to the corporation.
This was something which the government itself wished to see included in the bill so that it would not be obliged to come back to parliament to enlarge the responsibilities of Air Canada. It exemplifies an attitude which the administration has so often taken. Ministers opposite prefer passing orders-in-council to the parliamentary process. In many ways the actions they have taken amount to a sell-out of the parliamentary process, and clause 6(2) is a fine example.
Going back to the year 1972 we find that something like 3,326 orders in council were passed, only 653 of which were published in the Canada Gazette. This is cause for alarm and consternation among those of us who want to preserve and enhance the parliamentary process. It amounts to an abuse of the order in council procedure inasmuch as it is a circumvention of the parliamentary process.
We see evidence of this approach in other areas. There is a committee going around the country dealing with the subject of national unity. We in this party said it ought to be a parliamentary committee so that concerned individuals throughout Canada could speak directly to their elected representatives and feel they were participating in our democratic process. That is why I am so encouraged that the Senate should have seen fit to return this bill with clause 6(2) eliminated from it. Among other things, it shows the value of the Senate, whose members have a very useful role to play in

January 31, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
our democratic process. I commend them for amending the bill in this way.
I wish now to underline some of the points made by my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) when he was dealing with some of the facilities available at Edmonton international airport, specifically the customs service and preclearance services. We have been allocated $500,000 to construct these temporary facilities. At one time we were given a commitment that some $22 million would be spent on upgrading. This is the year of the Commonwealth Games. As was pointed out by my hon. friend, it is essential there should be facilities at Edmonton airport to accommodate the visitors which are expected.
I should like to reinforce the proposal made by my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) give an undertaking to United States firms that we shall have the necessary facilities at the airport, and in a year or two, permanent facilities for customs and preclearance, so the services needed for the Commonwealth Games will be there at least on a temporary basis this year.
To come back to Bill C-3, we in this party generally support the legislation. We feel it will serve our national air carrier well, enabling Air Canada, in turn, to serve the general public better.
Motion agreed to, amendments read the second time and concurred in.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to introduce for third reading Bill C-2, the fishing and recreational harbours
Fishing and Recreational Harbours act. This act will provide the necessary legislative authority to develop and administer commercial fishing and recreational harbours in Canada in order to meet the changing requirements of the fisheries and the growing needs of sports fishing and recreational boating. We have about 2,300 of these small harbours located across the country, with some comprising several wharves, breakwaters, and other structures, totalling some 4,000 facilities.
[ Translation]
We often forget that one of the essential factors of successful fisheries is precisely the development of harbour, and harbour facilities well situated in relation to fishing areas and providing standards required by fishermen as far as facilities and services are concerned. The provisions of Bill C-2 on development provide various measures which will meet those requirements as far as possible. The government will thus be in a position to continue to build, maintain and operate fishing harbours giving priority to such activities in the allotment of budget funds.

During debate on second reading of the bill some members were critical of the amount of money being spent on the development and maintenance of our small craft harbours. I should like to put on the record a few facts and figures which I believe speak for themselves.
In the six years prior to the transfer of responsibility for this program to the Department of Fisheries, expenditures on fishing and recreational harbours varied from a low of about $8 million a year to a little over $13 million. This is in sharp contrast to expenditure levels in recent years. They have more than quadrupled in some years; for example, in 1973-74 expenditures amounted to about $22.3 million; in 1974-75 to about $30.6 million; in 1975-76 to about $28.8 million; in 1976-77 to about $42.7 million; and in 1977-78 we expect the amount to reach some $47 million.
In 1976-77, and again this year, we have made extensive use of funds provided by the federal labour-intensive program and the Canada Works program to undertake improvements and repairs to our fishing harbours. Our small craft harbours administration has provided on-site assistance and materials required by communities, whilst utilizing local labour. This melding of small craft harbour resources with the federal labour-intensive and Canada manpower programs has resulted in the provision of additional funds for harbour development in the amount of nearly $32 million over the two years which would not have been otherwise available.
In terms of job creation, these special programs have meant some 7,500 more man-months in 1976-77, and we anticipate about 15,000 more man-months this year. The economic and social impact of these programs is very considerable as they are undertaken in communities with a high level of unemployment and have a multiplier effect in stimulating economic activity at the local level.
I have mentioned the substantial increase in levels of program expenditures in recent years, and I would now like to
2414

January 31, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours highlight a few of the more important considerations concerning the distribution of these funds.
It must be remembered that in 1973 the department inherited over 2,000 harbours and wharves, very large numbers of which were in dire need of repairs as a result of neglect in the past. Because of this, our programs have focused on making good this backlog of repairs and providing for only the most urgent of harbour expansions. It is only now that we are in a position to change the main thrust of our programs from repairs to that of improving, expanding and up-dating our harbours, and providing the better services needed by fishermen such as lighting, haulouts and proper work areas.
In 1973 we initiated a series of major studies to evaluate the existing fishing and recreational harbours owned by the federal government and to suggest a rationale for their development in the future. These studies were completed in 1975 and provide the basis for our ongoing plans, ensuring a planned and orderly undertaking of harbour improvements which are in step with the needs of the fishery across the country. The programming of projects each year takes into account not only the local needs of the fishermen but also the broader requirements and priorities of the commercial fishery throughout a region.
Our projects, whilst based on the needs of a community, are integrated within a national program in which major projects are usually phased over two or more years. This causes peaks in some regional allotments for the years covering major construction as they shift from region to region. For example, expenditures in Quebec peaked during 1975-76 and 1976-77 due to the special St. Lawrence fishing harbour development program, and have now been reduced to more modest levels. Meanwhile, expenditures in British Columbia will be increased this year and in the next few years as a result of construction of the new fishing harbour at Steveston, which is a very major undertaking. And so it goes in other regions.
Members of the House who have been following Bill C-2 through committee are aware of the misunderstandings that have arisen over provisions in the legislation which would allow introduction of a system of annual charges to commercial fishermen. This, naturally, has caused concern on the part of members on both sides of the House as to possible additional burdens being imposed on already hard-pressed fishermen.
This misconception, of course, is that the existing system is not imposing hardship. It is, because fishermen are not being treated equally at our harbours; at one they are required to pay a fee, and at others they are not. Inadequate administration and management of our harbours has resulted in that inequity, and others, that must be resolved.
However, let me assure the House that no decision has been made in respect of the details of a new fee structure. Fishermen are not going to wake up with the passage of this legislation to find they have to pay the federal government "X" number of dollars.
I believe we should continue with our present system, with all its shortcomings, for the present, without making any

changes until the health of the fishery improves and subsidies in that area are reduced. What we intend to do now is discuss with fishermen and their organizations how we can achieve a modest and equitable fee structure that would allow both better management of facilities and better on-site services for Canada's commercial fishermen. Certainly I cannot emphasize this enough. Any fee structure arrived at through that consultative process will be of a modest nature and will be phased in gradually in relation to the recovery of the stocks and the over-all health of the fishery.
The nucleus of the proposal we will bring to the fishermen is how we can best devise a fee system which will not only recognize market demand and relate to the level and quality of services provided, but will recognize regional differences. Obviously that means we are not going to be illogical enough, particularly in the case of east coast fishermen, to subsidize on the one hand and take it back through an unreasonable fee structure on the other.
I am confident that through discussion and consultation, and by approaching the issue with the best interests of the fishermen in mind, a system can be devised which will make history of existing inequities and provide only benefits to the fishermen in the future.
I want to say very simply that the purpose of this act is not to increase general revenues of the Receiver General of Canada, but rather is an attempt to put in place an administrative framework which in fact services the fishermen. The fishing and recreational harbours act will provide the legislative authority to undertake this type of work, and will also place emphasis on joint planning and co-operation with the provinces. I will, therefore, be introducing some new programs which will be responsive to provincial and municipal governments for the joint development of launching ramps and marinas where they are required to meet the needs of communities.
The bulk of pleasure boating activity is concentrated in Ontario and British Columbia and it has caused acute congestion within the harbours in these regions. I would, therefore, expect to see our expenditures continue to be directed primarily, but by no means entirely, to these areas of the country.
I should like to say in conclusion that this bill, the fishing and recreational harbours act, is important to ensure the proper continuing development of fishing and recreational harbours in the country. It will allow the minister to introduce new programs and administrative arrangements which are responsive to the changing needs of our commercial fishermen and recreational boaters. I thank hon. members on both sides of the House for their co-operation, as well as their valuable comments and suggestions made during the review of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-2, an act respecting the administration and development of certain fishing and recreational harbours in Canada. This bill was introduced first in the last session. At that time it was known as Bill C-7.
January 31, 1978

Unfortunately the Liberal government chose to treat this as an unimportant piece of legislation, so unimportant in fact that it chose to let it die on the order paper. Yet during that period of time the government passed legislation relating to the Canada Lands Surveys Act, diplomatic and consular privileges, an income tax agreement with Germany and some 12 name changes to constituencies.
I am not saying these pieces of legislation were not important, but I am questioning their relative importance vis-a-vis fisheries. Surely the government's handling of Bill C-7 demonstrates its lack of concern for the Canadian fishing industry, an industry where the gross annual cash receipts to our primary producers now total approximately $400 million, with an annual market value of approximately $1 billion. Our annual commercial fish landings of close to one million tons are approximately one-tenth of those of the leading producer of food from water, namely, Japan. It is between 1 per cent and 2 per cent of the world's production. Obviously Canada has a long way to go. There is a lot of opportunity if we get out the nets and get to work.
Because of the fate of Bill C-7, my colleagues and I, in a spirit of co-operation, allowed the government to send Bill C-2 directly to committee at the beginning of this session. Unfortunately this spirit of co-operation at the beginning of the new session ended in committee where the Liberal majority refused to accept sound amendments aimed at improving this bill. In particular, the Liberal majority supported those sections of the bill which will increase licence fees, which will not ensure consultation with interested parties, and which will give the minister the right arbitrarily to lease harbours to any one person. Bill C-2 updates past legislation and regulations pertaining to small craft harbours.
Legislative authority for the administration of these harbours has been provided by the government's Harbours and Piers Act, its accompanying government wharves regulations and various orders in council. The Harbours and Piers Act was originally drafted in 1895 and revised in 1937. Obviously years ago fisheries were not considered that important, because when we look at 1895 and 1937, we find a lot of bridge has gone over the water in Halifax, for example in the time elapsed. As a result, it has not focused on the present day administration needs of the fishermen and recreational boaters. As well, it does not include provisions for the development of these harbours. New legislation has been needed for some time. At last we have Bill C-2 which will gather, consolidate, and update the scattered elements under one new act.
In addition, when the program and administrative responsibilities for the small craft harbours were transferred to the Department of Fisheries and the Environment in June 1973 from the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport, it was done so by an order in council. This method of transfer has not been as effective for the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) as legislative enactment. For example, one Department of Transport official on the west coast refused to acknowledge the transfer and he did not send his files to the Department of Fisheries and the
Fishing and Recreational Harbours Environment until late last year, some three years after the time of transfer. Perhaps the minister takes exception to that, but that is my information.
Nevertheless, in spite of these good intentions, Bill C-2 raises some questions and problems. The budget of the small craft harbours branch, which will administer Bill C-2, was only $35 million in fiscal year 1976-77. Most of that money was used for the repair and modernization of the federal government's fishing and recreational harbours and wharves on the east and west coasts. This is a pitifully small amount of money when one considers that the small craft harbours branch has responsibility over some 2,300 facilities.
I have been informed that the government would like to abandon or destroy about half of these facilities. Consequently, it would appear that the Liberal government's master plan is not to increase expenditures to meet the number of facilities, but to decrease the number of facilities to meet the expenditures, regardless of whether they are serving the needs of communities. I made this point last December and indicated that, if my analysis was incorrect, then the minister should table the future plans of the small craft harbours branch so that they could be discussed in committee. I am still waiting. The longer I wait, the more credible is my original analysis.
At the same time, the number of fishery wharves has been decreasing. These wharves are essential to the very livelihood of many maritime Canadians. This government has become more involved in the financing and construction of recreational harbours. This drift toward recreation at the expense of Fishing raises a valid question as to whether the Department of Fisheries and the Environment is fulfilling its mandate. Its mandate is to promote and undertake programs designed to improve the management and sustained economic utilization of the marine and aquatic renewable resources of the nation, compatible with a concern for the quality of the environment. I hope the minister will reconsider his priorities, because after all there is a Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo), a minister who could be made responsible for the development of recreational facilities.
Nonetheless, since Bill C-2 is partly concerned with financing recreational harbours, one still might question one aspect of the government's marina assistance program which was established to encourage the construction of new marinas by local municipalities and by private developers. The federal government pays for the construction of the breakwater and for dredging, while the municipality and/or developer pays the other costs plus upkeep. Federal government participation is limited to 50 per cent of the total cost of the marina. However, despite paying up to 50 per cent of the cost, it receives no future compensation for its contribution. Why should private developers line their pockets with taxpayers' money? I hope the government ensures that the marina is opened and available to all boaters at reasonable cost.
Unfortunately the figures referred to by the minister this evening are not the same as those contained in his news release of December 15, 1977, which announced spending under FLIP. I am sure my constituents wonder what is going on when they

hear the many different alphabetical acronyms which are being used, such as FLIP, LIP and zippety-do-dahs. On December 15 the minister announced that $18,386,000 would be spent over the next nine months for fisheries management and small craft harbours projects. Frankly, this is something we have been advocating for considerable time. We have been saying it is not necessary to spend millions of dollars to find out what is needed in Atlantic Canada because we have many wharves, skidways and harbour facilities that require improvement. We welcome additional money. But I say to the minister that it still only brings the total for harbours in Canada to date to something a little more than $50 million-$35 million in the estimates and the $18 million.
When I look at the money spent on Mirabel, something in the nature of $600 million to $800 million, the total amount spent on harbours would cover perhaps a couple of runways. It still falls far short of the amount we hand out to run the Post Office, the deficit of which this year will be something like $475 million. We seem to think nothing of funding the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to the tune of something like $468 million this year, or over $9 million a week. When we look, as I said a moment ago, at an industry that is worth $400 million to Canadians, to the primary sector alone, and $1 billion in total, I submit it is time that the industry received greater consideration from this government. Since the number of fisheries wharves has also been decreasing, we would like to see a little more action, especially in some parts of Nova Scotia.
So much for the good news. The major faults of this bill so far as I can determine-and we gave the bill very careful study in committee-lie in the areas of leasing, consultation and licence fees. Clauses 5 and 8 of the bill read as follows:
5. (1) The minister may undertake projects for the acquisition, development, construction, improvement or repair of any scheduled harbour or any fishing or recreational harbour to which this act applies.
8. The minister may, subject to the regulations,
(a)	lease any scheduled harbour or any part thereof to any person;
(b)	grant a licence to any person for the use of any scheduled harbour or any
part thereof; and
(c)	enter into an agreement with the government of any province or agency
thereof for the occupancy and use of any scheduled harbour or any part
thereof.
I said in committee that these powers are too wide for the minister. They are too wide for any minister. We cannot understand how any minister can believe that he has the right to lease a harbour to any one person. We do not believe that fishermen should needlessly be subjected to the whims of a private individual or corporation who may wish to lease the harbour. In committee we introduced an amendment which would have required that any leasing be done to provincial or municipal government. However, the Liberal majority voted this down.
We also fear that the bill does not provide for sufficient consultation between the minister and the affected parties. According to the small craft harbours branch, Bill C-2 is wide

enough to sail the Queen Mary through. It is wide enough for the minister to go it alone where he can work, if he so wishes, in concert with the provinces and municipalities. The trouble with this minister is that he does not often choose to work with the provinces.
I can see problems with clause 5 of this bill which allows the minister to build recreational harbours wherever he chooses without regard for provincial or municipal desires. I should like to ask the minister what has happened to the view that the provinces should be consulted on matters affecting their interests. I say to the minister most sincerely that his lack of consultation with the provincial ministers over fisheries matters has been a major criticism of him. The Halifax Chronicle Herald has contained nothing but criticism of him for months, as expressed by the provincial minister of Newfoundland and by the supporter of his own party in the province of Nova Scotia, the provincial minister of fisheries in our province.
This lack of consultation was especially evident last session at committee hearings on Bill C-38, to amend the Fisheries Act. Province after province came forward from the Atlantic to the Pacific, from Nova Scotia to British Columbia, and each and every brief presented before that committee contained a condemnation of this minister for lack of consultation with them on the bill's provision for fighting pollution. Stonewalling tactics do not work. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that confrontation will never replace consultation, and that we do not need to wonder why there is dissatisfaction and discontent at present throughout the land.
Unfortunately it would appear that the minister has learned very little from his experience with Bill C-38, because in committee his colleagues refused to support our amendment which would have required him at least to consult with the affected provinces and municipalities before constructing a small craft harbour. I had hoped the minister would have learned from the past that he can no longer treat the provinces and municipalities as mere pawns which exist to obey and carry out the programs and policies of this minister and his staff; but it would seem from the Liberal attitude which was displayed in the committee that this government will try to continue to ride roughshod over the provinces' and municipalities' rights and desires.
Our major disappointment at the committee hearings centred around the minister's attitude toward licence fees for the use of small craft harbour facilities. The bill allows the minister to set whatever fee he wants without having to go to parliament for approval. The minister admitted that a licence fee would be imposed for the use of government small craft harbour facilities, but he was unwilling to tell us what that fee would be. Rather than that, he stated, we should pass the bill immediately so that he could set up a fee structure.
This is like closing the barn door after the horse has escaped. If we were to pass this bill unaltered, I submit we would be derelict in our duties because the minister could then establish a fee structure and remain unresponsive to any criticisms or suggestions for its improvement. I have learned that a plan is now being discussed which would require a
January 31, 1978

fisherman to purchase a licence based upon the length of his vessel, possibly $1 per foot, although this was not clarified this evening by the minister in his remarks. He simply stated that fishermen should not worry that they would wake up and find they would have to pay X number of dollars after we pass this bill.
I say to the minister that fishermen wake up many nights wondering in some cases where their next dollar is coming from, whether the weather will be fine the next day, whether they can go to sea, whether there will be any lobsters there for them to catch. Now he has given them another worry: will it be $1 or $2? How many dollars per foot will he charge them? Will the minister deign to tell them this evening? He says that this fee will only cover the use of the government's small craft harbour facilities. There will still be other fees to pay, such as a licence fee for lobster fishermen or for ground fishermen, or a licence fee for tying up the boat. The fishermen with whom I have spoken recently say: "We are getting to be like the office of Sun Life, filled with all kinds of papers delivered to us from bureaucratic Ottawa. We will soon have to get an accountant just to keep track of our licences".
What I said last December still holds true. In my view this proposal for a licence fee is simply another unfair tax on Canadians using public facilities in Atlantic Canada, while people in more prosperous parts of this nation are provided more public facilities free of charge.
