My colleagues from western Canada are quite capable of speaking for themselves. I am speaking for the fishermen in Atlantic Canada, and primarily for people in my province of Nova Scotia. I would like to think that after 21 years here in June I have a fairly good idea of what they like and dislike about some of these fisheries policies.
I contend that what is being proposed in this legislation- and I regret that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is not here because I do not like to speak about ministers in their absence-is nothing more than the concept put forward by the Minister of Transport, the user-pay concept, and I submit that it is not acceptable in Atlantic Canada. A $50 fee for a 50-foot boat may not sound like much to the minister or to an Ottawa bureaucrat, but to an Atlantic fisherman $50 can sometimes be a very princely sum not too easily come by, especially in these times of high unemployment.
In my view it is senseless for the government to talk about added licence fees and added financial burdens during these times of high unemployment. On a national basis in December unemployment was running at 8.5 per cent, up from 7.5 per cent the year before. The figures were even worse in Atlantic Canada. There the average stood at 13.3 per cent or 107,000 unemployed persons, up from 10.8 per cent or 90,000 the year
Fishing and Recreational Harbours before. In effect, one worker in eight is without employment in Atlantic Canada.
On a provincial basis unemployment in December stood at 17.5 per cent, or 31,000 people, in Newfoundland; in Prince Edward Island it stood at 11.4 per cent, or 5,000 people; in Nova Scotia it stood at 10.2 per cent, or 33,000 people; and in New Brunswick it stood at 14.3 per cent, or 38,000 people. Worse still, these figures are expected to increase. By 1979 another 12,000 people are projected to be unemployed in Atlantic Canada, and most of them will be residents of Newfoundland where unemployment is projected to increase by a full 3 per cent over the next two years. These are only bare statistics. In terms of human sorrow and mental anguish the story is much worse. Yet this government insists upon licence fees, causing the people of Atlantic Canada who can least afford it to bear an even heavier share of the burden of the mismanagement of the economy of Canada by this Liberal government. speechtext:
An hon. member opposite says we are laughing. Well, he can sit over there and laugh at the fishermen of Atlantic Canada. He can laugh at the hardships they face and the work they have to do to make a living in a very harsh environment. He can laugh if he wishes. But it is no laughing matter in Atlantic Canada, and if the hon. member wants to see how funny it is, he can come down to Atlantic Canada some time.
The minister has argued that fishermen already face licence fees because there are already wharfage charges on the books. However, as there are only approximately 200 wharfingers throughout Canada to collect those charges, most fishermen have grown accustomed to using government wharves and small craft harbour facilities free of charge. The minister plans to revamp the wharfinger system so that all major small craft harbours will be under the administration of wharfingers. As I understand it, some 1,466 facilities have no wharfingers, and the number hired has no relation to the number of small craft harbours in a province. Newfoundland, for example, has only eight. In Nova Scotia I understand that there are about 40, while Quebec has only five.
In committee my colleagues and I simply requested the minister, bearing in mind the high unemployment levels and the low income levels of Atlantic Canada, to defer any introduction of a licence fee for at least five years. After five years, in our opinion the Atlantic fishery should hopefully be on its way to recovery. It should be on its way to recovery because of the phase-out of foreign fishing within the 200-mile economic zone. In this phase-out decreased fishing should enable fish stocks to rebuild automatically. As Progressive Conservatives this seemed to us to be a reasonable compromise. However, the minister and all the Liberal members on that committee voted down that compromise. They will have to answer to the people

January 31, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
of Atlantic Canada for so doing. They refused that reasonable request.
As a result of the minister's refusal to take a compromising position over licence fees, we on this side are forced to vote against this bill. We are very much aware of the economic suffering which many of our fishermen have been going through. For example, five years ago approximately 7 per cent of Canada's commercial fishermen earned less than $7,500, which is the generally accepted poverty line figure. I do not believe that this figure has changed drastically, especially with reduced catch quotas. Therefore, I feel that Canadian fishermen should not be subjected at this time to additional erosions of their already small incomes.
Speaking as one who has lived a lifetime on the ocean, I am well aware that a watertight, seaworthy ship can travel over thousands of miles of ocean without facing any serious difficulty. However, when a little water enters the ship the crew is in difficulty, and when a lot of water enters the ship the crew is in danger of foundering and sinking with that ship. The present Liberal government can be compared somewhat to a ship in the ocean. As long as it made laws for Canadians which could serve as a guide for their day-to-day social, cultural and business activities, the ship of state could safely sail over the economic ocean of Canada. However, this government, unfortunately, has not been satisfied at all with doing the job it was elected to do. It not only wanted to sail over Canada's economic ocean; it started leaking economic water into the Canadian ship of state. Just as a ship sinks when it takes in too much of the element over which it is sailing, so too is the Canadian ship of state sinking, because this government today is taking in too much of the economic ocean of Canada.
For safety's sake, the water of the ocean must be kept out of a ship; and for the safe and sound development of the Canadian economy this government must stick to the job of manning the ship of state while allowing the economic oceans of Canada to rise, fall and move as the currents of individual ambition and initiative strive to develop and improve conditions individually and collectively. We on this side do not want to see Canada's ship of state founder and sink, but this is what is happening as this government seeks to make laws and to set up too strong a control over the economy through the setting up of government controlled companies which ultimately destroy the freedoms of individual Canadians and limits their right to make meaningful decisions.
This is what we see happening today with this bill. This bill seeks to tax Canadian fishermen further. It seeks to limit their freedom of choice as it applies to docking their ships, and it ultimately will give more political power over the lives of individual Canadians to the government. The appointment of some 1,400 wharfingers alone would be pork barrelling of the worst kind. It would give power to the minister unlike anything we have seen. This is not restraint. This is not restriction of bureaucracy. This is an expansion of it.
In conclusion, if we are to break out from under the present heavy burden of excessive taxation, mounting inflation and rising unemployment, we can do so only by giving free rein to

individual ambition and initiative. We must encourage the individual Canadian to do better, and this cannot be accomplished by further restricting his individual freedoms and increasing his tax burdens.
In the recent joint provincial fisheries development proposal there was no reference whatsoever to Bill C-2. The proposal did, however, deal with the resource fleet development, markets and foreign arrangements, something which the minister has chosen, in discussing this bill, to ignore completely. As a result of the minister's attitude an entire generation of young Canadian fishermen may well be lost unless licenses and boats are made available. In parts of Atlantic Canada many young people who want to go fishing are forced to turn elsewhere for employment. Many have skipper's licenses but no boats, and fishermen can no longer afford to build boats on their own. Because it is imperative that we build up the inshore fleet, the federal government should make funds available for fishermen who wish to borrow.
Canadian shipyard costs are much higher than in Europe. The fishermen have to sell their catches in European as well as American markets on a competitive basis. It is up to this government to arrange the equalizer between our own costs and European costs so that our fleet can be built up for the benefit of Canadian shipyards and the industry.
The most recent statement the minister made to me did nothing to indicate that some of the problems to which I refer will be resolved or even studied, so at this time we therefore feel it necessary to vote against this bill on third reading.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not long since this bill was first before us that it is not surprising there was some uncertainty this evening about whether we would be debating it or Bill C-17. Until the last minute it was not clear whether we would be going ahead with Bill C-3, Bill C-2 or Bill C-17. This is a further example of the disorder in which this government finds itself. It was only at the last minute they decided to move Bill C-2.
Bill C-2 was originally presented as Bill C-7, but that was long ago. It was thoroughly examined in committee both as Bill C-7 and as Bill C-2 and the government eventually responded to recommendations from this side to modify some of the plans laid out in the bill. Nonetheless, the terms were left in the bill to enable the government to go back and do something they said they were going to withdraw for the time being. I refer, of course, to the levying of fees for the use of the facilities.
Fishing on the west coast is in complete disarray at the moment, despite the fact that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) is Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. Fishermen are in revolt against the regulations that have been brought forward, against the uncertainty of plans for licensing, against the thought that they will be charged the financial schedule that was being proposed. Although we heard during the committee
January 31, 1978

proceedings that they had been consulted before the fee schedule was brought forward, this has since turned out to be misleading. There was no consultation until these regulations were brought down in committee. Then we found a series of regulations drawn up without regard to the fact that fees for licensing on the west coast ranged up to about $2,000 and fees for the use of harbours on the west coast were to be double the fees on the east coast.
This is unacceptable in a country where equalization is supposed to be one of the features of our society. There ought to be some means of maintaining unity in this country. Why exacerbate matters by surcharging the west coast on fees, thereby aggravating the disunifying factors that are already there. These are some of the reasons why I must vote against the bill.
Clause 9(f) of the bill reads as follows:
The Governor in Council may make regulations ...
(0 prescribing charges for the use of any scheduled harbour;
An earlier clause designates scheduled harbours. When the bill is passed the minister will have power to prescribe the fees. We have the word of the minister in committee. I take his word as he is an honourable man, but supposing he should not be the minister one day. We hear there are other more exalted roles for him to play.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: I am going to B.C.!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
The minister expresses an interest in going to B.C. I think he would have trouble there. With the suggestions he has made about overcharging the fishermen in B.C. I do not think they would accept him too readily.
We have an undertaking by a minister in committee, however, that he will not for the moment prescribe charges for the use of any scheduled harbour. Under the provisions of clause 9 the minister may do certain things through the governor in council. About fifteen different things will be proposed by his officials, be approved by the minister and then go to the governor in council. If another minister takes over he may, of course, scrap the undertaking given by this minister and introduce the fees that were withdrawn.
I was absolutely staggered by the schedule of fees presented to us in committee by officials of the department. I think it was that as much as anything that caused me to have serious doubts about the bill and which brought me to the conclusion that I shall have to vote against it.
I mentioned the disarray of the fishing industry on the west coast. A former minister of the environment in this government devised a scheme of restricting licenses, presumably with a view to the management of the stock of the fisheries. He introduced two different kinds of fishing licenses and this scheme has continued. For reasons best known to the fishermen and the minister, this system just has not worked. Today, in an open meeting, I asked whether the Davis plan for managing the catch had resulted in increased stock on the west coast. The answer from knowledgeable scientific people was
Fishing and Recreational Harbours that it had not. Now I understand that the minister had decided the plan will not work and has appointed a Mr. Sol Sinclair to investigate the AB licensing system to determine whether it should be modified in order to produce an increase in stock or whether some other system would be preferable. Meanwhile, the fishermen do not know where the licensing system is going to lead. As I say, they are in disarray.
Another aspect of this bill has me worried. In clauses 10, 8 and 5, there are possibilities for patronage. In fact, possibilities for patronage abound in this bill. Clause 10 states:
-the Minister may designate as an enforcement officer any person who is, in the opinion of the Minister, qualified to be so designated-
There is no indication of what the qualifications ought to be. If the minister intended that a fisheries officer, RCMP officer or coast guard officer should be designated as an enforcement officer under the meaning of this act, why did he not clearly state that? The qualifications of an enforcement officer ought to be somewhere. There is a definition, but no qualification. This is very dangerous.
After the next election, there will be a lot of defeated candidates. Some of them will be designated if this minister is still the minister, which I doubt.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: He will be.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
If he is here, he will have to change sides. He will no longer be fisheries minister. Some of these people opposite might have it in mind to designate defeated candidate enforcement officers. That option, of course, will be foreclosed with the next election. There is no doubt in my mind about that. The same option is open to the minister under clause 8, which states:
The minister may-
(a) lease any scheduled harbour ... to any person;
A scheduled harbour may have a great commercial potential. The danger here is that a long lease may be signed before the next election. The minister may feel that it is about time someone was looked after, and in order to ensure his vote at the next election he will lease one of the harbours that he has scheduled to that individual. That is another opportunity for patronage. Bill C-2 ought to be called the patronage bill.
Clause 5(1)-and this, Mr. Speaker, you will find hard to believe-states:
The Minister may undertake projects for the acquisition, development, construction, improvement or repair of any scheduled harbour or any fishing or recreational harbour to which this Act applies.
The minister better make use of that before the election if he intends to compensate those who have given good service to the party. Clause 5(3) provides a beautiful opportunity. You would not believe this one. I quote:
The Minister may ... enter into an agreement with any person to provide for
(a) the undertaking jointly with the person of any project that the Minister is
authorized to undertake under subsection (1);

January 31, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
Would you believe that? It is open to pork barrelling of the worst possible kind. We are being asked to approve the possibility of government, whichever government, authorizing pork barrelling. That is something that is normally done under the counter without legislative backup, but here we are being asked to make it legal. This 1 will not do.
In his introduction the minister talked about fees. I have already mentioned them in my few remarks. He stated that for the time being there are not going to be any fees. He said they are going to study the question again. I do not have the text of the minister's comments in front of me, but he left the impression that this is all being done out of his good nature. Someone happened to mention to him that there was some inconsistency in the fees being proposed. Out of his good nature, and he is a good natured guy, he said he would withdraw the fee schedule.
It was not withdrawn because of his consultations with the fishermen. It was because of all the harping we did in committee. We stated that they were impossible fee schedules and we were not going to have them. Thereupon they were withdrawn for the time being. However, as I already stated, the provision is still in the bill for him to impose that fee schedule whenever he wishes.
The other problem on the west coast is the enhancement program. It is such a complicated matter that I am not sure I will be able to deal with it in all aspects. It has gone a little foul in two regards. One suggestion is that the enhancement program is going to be contracted out. I have heard, and this distresses me, that some fisheries officials have decided there is more to be gained outside the public service by taking a contract to do the enhancement program than there is inside using fisheries officers. I do not like that suggestion.
The enhancement program requires the most careful, scientific care of trained people. The minister would not contract out to me, even if I were on his side of the House, because I am not scientifically trained.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: Oh yes, I would.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Although we are good friends, I do not think he would go quite that far. I know I am not trained to carry out the program. If it goes to contracting out, how is the minister to determine whether those he contracts to carry out the program are qualified to do so? This provision is very dangerous. The minister is about to say he would only hire those already in his service who decide to retire. That is a very bad principle. It is one of the aspects that is causing a great deal of concern on the west coast.
The other matter of concern is the cost of the enhancement program. It was to be included in the fees. If this minister has anything to do with it-and he will not be the minister for all time-it will be included in the fees when that schedule comes forward. That is how the salmon enhancement program should work. Instead of user-pay, or "user-pray," I think that "prey on the user" is the correct way of defining the program. The western fishermen will have none of that.

I have gone into some of the regulations. Under this bill there are two sets of regulations. We have reached a point in this parliament at which we are considering bills whose purpose is to provide a framework within which regulations may be set. That is the way the government operates. They will not come clean and say what regulations they intend to establish. Clause 9 and clause 25 each implies different sets of regulations. Clause 9 gives the governor in council authority to make regulations governing 15 different matters, including fees, schedules, safety and so on. Fair enough. But the officials surely know what ought to be contained in these regulations. Why not append them to the bill? We criticized the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) when we were dealing with another bill and eventually we got the regulations appended to the measure. That is the way it should work.
There is no question that regulations are required and that they cannot all be written into an act. But they could be attached as a schedule. The schedule could be brought forward for consideration during the life of an act and altered at that time. Blanket authority should not be given to officials to draw up regulations which are not known to the House in advance.
Clause 25 contemplates that the governor-in-council may by regulation designate any offence under the act. Here we are dealing with the fixing of fines by another set of regulations. Surely it should be possible to append the regulations to a bill so that we and the fishermen directly concerned may know exactly where we stand. The matter is even more important to the fishermen than it is to us; we are trying to defend their interests in our comments tonight.
My hon. friend from South Shore (Mr. Crouse) mentioned the wharfingers and the possibility of patronage. I shall not develop that aspect, but is the minister planning to designate some of the wharfingers as enforcement officers? Maybe. Maybe not. I am sorry there is no clearer definition of what is meant by "enforcement officer". The term could apply to wharfingers; they have certain powers under the act which are stronger than one might be prepared to accept at first glance.
My final comments relate to the 200-mile limit which is another source of great confusion on both coasts because of the uncertainty and the secrecy surrounding the negotiations between ourselves and the United States with regard to the definition of our boundaries at the four places where our two zones meet. There has been no report on these negotiations. We know that a competent diplomat has been assigned to the task backed by a good staff, but we are expected to take so much on trust when the government has given us no reason for extending that trust. It worries me that we should be expected to extend trust to a government which has shown itself incapable of governing this country. On the contrary, it is seemingly determined to break the country up. Still, we are asked to trust the government to conclude satisfactory agreements with our neighbour to the south on the boundary between the two zones. We do not even know what possibilities are being explored by the negotiators.
January 31, 1978

In this connection, I note that my former colleague, Marcel Cadieux, is the principal negotiator. I have great trust in the man. But why should he not have behind him the authority of parliament to get what is required by Canada in these negotiations? Why has there not been a briefing, even a confidential briefing, given to selected members of parliament? They would not go blabbing. Members of the Press Gallery would try to get information. Bless them, let them try. But in matters of this importance there could not be any possibility of leakage.
A further cause of uncertainty is that no provision whatever has been made for the surface patrol of a tremendously large area which was taken under our umbrella on January 1, 1977. I do not know whether the minister, when he was out in Victoria, saw those ships, boats, or whatever they are, which are intended to be our patrol vessels. For their size and number they do a fair job but they cannot be expected to carry Canadian jurisdiction to the extent of 200 miles or even, on the west coast, to the 50-mile margin which is the end of the fishing limit out there to all intents and purposes. This still leaves a lot of sea to be covered.
The three vessels out there, the Runner, the Racer and the Rider, are just not capable of the task assigned to them, and there is still nothing in the works, as far as I can make out, unless something is being negotiated with Denmark on a charter basis. And that would be a great shame when we have within this country the competence, the technology, to produce our own fisheries patrol vessels. They ought to be on the stocks. Is any thought at all being given to that? I see the minister nods but I have not seen any tenders for design being let, or anything like that. I believe he is keeping that in his head because he does not want me to know that vessels intended for us on the west coast are not being built on the west coast. Vessels which are for use on the Pacific coast should be designed and built on the Pacific coast whether they are for naval or for fisheries use.

speechtext:
And at Saint John for the east coast; we shall split it for the Arctic.
It is on these grounds-the uncertainty due to what the regulations will contain, the uncertainty as to what the level of the fees will be, the uncertainty into which the west coast fishermen have been locked because of the licensing system and the patronage potential contained in the bill-that we find it impossible to support this bill.
In addition there is the salmonoid program, which had been the enhancement program to which I subscribed. I do not like the way it is going. Last but not least, there is the failure of this bill to define exactly what is intended by an enforcement officer. For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, 1 do feel that it will be impossible for my colleagues and I to support this bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on
Fishing and Recreational Harbours this bill, particularly after listening to my colleague from the west coast. I had heard the party opposite described as the party of gloom and doom, but nowhere is that more evident than in debate of this bill tonight. It seems to me that this is one area, not the only area in the country, where there is room for hope, yet all we have heard are the negative aspects of this particular industry.
My colleague from the west coast has told me that the west coast fisheries are in disarray. There is disillusionment, discouragement and despair in that region. I do not know what the mood is there because I cannot speak for the west coast, but I can tell you that in my part of the east coast, in the Atlantic area, there is optimism, there is buoyancy and there is a spirit among the fishermen which has never been experienced before. All of this is due to the policies of the government and this minister. That is a fact. If you would like to go and talk to the fishermen, Mr. Speaker, they will tell you the same things I am telling you now. I have heard the comment that all of this is as a result of the policies of this minister. This minister is known not necessarily as the minister of fisheries but as the minister of fishermen. There is a great difference, and there is adequate evidence why that should be so.
I heard arguments earlier this evening concerning the amount of money put in to small craft harbours compared with what was spent on Mirabel airport, what was spent on the CBC and whatever. Some years ago when the Koreans hit the U.S. market with cheap hake, something like $140 million was gained by this minister from the government of Canada to support a failing Atlantic fishery, which was failing through no fault of its own but through the fault of the state of the marketplace at that time. So when hon. members fault the minister for obtaining insufficient money for the fishery, there is evidence there to contradict that. When they fault him for not bringing in policies that are in the interests of the fishermen, here is a minister who put money into the fishermen's pocket. The subsidies up to two years ago went to the companies. Now two and a half cents a pound on top quality groundfish is going into the pockets of the fishermen for the first time. This is the minister not of fisheries but of fishermen.
I want to make some comments concerning this bill. I think they have to be put in the context of the 200-mile limit. I was mystified because I heard that the 200-mile limit was not necessarily going over as a good thing. In my area it is the greatest thing since sliced bread. The 200-mile limit is a fantastic thing for this country. It is the greatest reason for hope that we have, and that is certainly true in my province. As a result of the 200-mile limit, quotas over-all have been decreased so that we are now rebuilding stocks, but Canadian quotas have increased. What is more important is the fact that the quota to inshore fishermen has increased, which comes off the top of the over-all quota before it is divided up. This is the point I want to zero in on. This bill is going to be good for the inshore fishery, which in my area is still the backbone of the fishery.

January 31, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
I want to refer to a statement made by the minister of external affairs, I believe last week. I would like to quote parts of it in a press release that accompanied his statement.
The guiding principle for future development of Newfoundland's fisheries should be that the inshore fishery comes first.
I cannot read all of what he said, but here are some other statements:
It is not a matter of having one or the other ... It is ... very much a question of balance, and in considering what that balance should be, there is now, near unanimous agreement on a fundamental first principle for fisheries development: the inshore fishery comes first.
First of all, if the inshore fishery is to be the backbone of the Newfoundland fishery-I do agree with that statement, and I believe it to be true certainly along the northeast coast-then we have a need for good shore facilities. This bill gives the minister management over those shore facilities and a structure for seeing those shore facilities are developed. In the long run that will benefit the fishermen. He makes provision, contrary to what we have heard, for consultation, for community involvement in the planning facilities. I do not know about other areas, but we have not had that in my area before. The opening is there for putting further staff in place. I can only speak again for the area I represent. It is a good thing as long as it does not become a rigid tier of bureaucracy. This is something we have to guard against.
If the minister is going to put in place this management regime and if he is going to recruit additional staff, I would urge the minister to have advisory groups set up among the fishermen in the same way that he does in setting his licensing policies. I believe that consultation has to be there. He has shown in the past that he is prepared to do it and I urge him to do it in the future.
As for the matter of charges to be levied, the minister has dealt with that in his own speech and there is no need for me to elaborate. Whatever the minister may do he has shown up to now that he is the minister of fishermen and that his policies have been in the interests, not only of the industry as a whole, but of the fishermen themselves. They know that whatever he may do he will act in their best interests, and he will not raise licence fees unnecessarily until such time as they are making an adequate income.
That adequate income is coming. This year I would say on the northeast coast of Newfoundland the increase in the amount of fish caught and the amount of money earned is something like 40 per cent over last year. The salaries are improving, not to the point where we would like to see them, but they are getting better. People are going back to the fishery who have not been in it for a long time. But I still do not think that we should be imposing two charges on fishermen, and this is something the minister will have to monitor.
There is something else I would like to mention, but we are running out of time. Better shore facilities go hand in hand with some measures that the Department of Fisheries have already taken regarding quality control. The wharves and breakwaters have to be in place. We have to build more of them, and we have built more of them. But regarding shore

facilities, we had to have measures such as the program we have put into effect on the northeast coast of Newfoundland.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can confirm that the continual practice of the leader of the House has been to respect the opinion of the opposition as concerns the legislative program. However, I believe that we must be flexible and understanding enough to recognize that there can be last minute changes. According to what I have been told, what has happened today is as follows, if I may have the attention of hon. members. During the question period, the parliamentary secretary to the minister concerned talked with the House leader of the opposition and also with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I see a member waving at me: we shall be able to have a talk after the late show this evening. At that time, Mr. Speaker, it was clearly stated that after studying Bill C-3, we would proceed this afternoon to the report stage of Bill C-2 and there was even some discussion with the House leader of the opposi-

tion and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre about the amendment which received unanimous consent this evening. I do not know if at that time it was understood that there would be a change in our program, but I want to say one thing: Last Thursday, when the government House leader announced the legislative program, he said that we would proceed this week to the study of Bills C-3, C-17 and C-2. Of course, if we consider what I have just said literally, normally Bill C-2 should have come after Bill C-17. A while ago, before rising on a point of order, the opposition leader talked to me and I suggested that he raise this question at the next private meeting of party leaders, which will probably be held Thursday as usual. At that time we might review the facts and perhaps make the necessary adjustments. In view of his point of order, I would ask to the opposition leader to demonstrate some flexibility. speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not want to participate in a debate at this time in the kind of fashion which has occurred. I think hon. members should be honourable, and the truth of the matter is: if a vote is called without an order and it is not a 15-minute bell, in many cases it is because there are members at meetings in this city who require 40 or 50 minutes to get to the chamber. That will occur time and time again if there is no notification in advance of a 15-minute bell. My understanding is that all House leaders have agreed to something. subtopic: HEALTH-ALLEGED DANGER TO INFANTS FROM CHEMICALS CARRIED BY NURSING MOTHERS-REQUEST FOR STUDY
HEALTH-ALLEGED DANGER TO INFANTS FROM CHEMICALS CARRIED BY NURSING MOTHERS-REQUEST FOR STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 14, 1977 I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) a question in the House concerning the alleged danger to infants from breast feeding, particularly by mothers whose milk contains high levels of DDT and PCBs, or polychlorinate biphenyls. The PCBs are industrial chemicals which pollute water and air, and eventually our food, and are found in higher levels than they should be in mothers' milk.
I am concerned about this and would like to know whether there is any correlation between the increase in levels of DDT and the weight of the patient. We know that DDT is stored in the fatty tissues of animals and fish. Suppose that one woman weighs a couple of hundred pounds and another one weighs 125 pounds, and suppose both women give birth. Does the mother who is obese carry more DDT and biphenyls in her body, and consequently in her breast milk with which she feeds her baby, than the thinner mother?
The second question I would like to put concerns lower levels of these substances found in cows' milk. I should like to know from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Robinson), who has been

interested in this kind of work for some time, what tests have been carried out on cows, whether on dairy cows or first calvers, and for what period of time. Could he also tell me whether any beef cows were tested, because there is a great difference between those two animals so far as storage of fat is concerned. I would like to know also whether we have a central laboratory where those tests can be carried out.
Statistics indicate that only about one in four mothers nurse their babies for various lengths of time. This is less than in the past and less than in undeveloped countries where babies are nursed for months.
I also have the following question and I wonder whether the department is prepared to do some research on it. Suppose a mother weighing 140 pounds goes on nursing her baby and then loses weight. Will the amount of DDT and biphenyls in her body accumulate or decrease? If it accumulates, it would be paramount for pediatricians to keep the weight of mothers at the same level so that they would not be storing DDT and biphenyls in their body fat. Does the government have facilities at present in any province in Canada for testing milk, and are there facilities for testing drugs which may have been ingested by mothers?
9 (2217)
One case which comes to my mind involved a woman who underwent a bone graft in her back. She had a degenerating spine. Unfortunately, she developed the morphine habit because of all the pain she experienced. She overcame the habit. She later had a baby, and I often wonder about this because there was some problem with that baby. I wonder if tests have been done.
Dr. Morrison mentioned that there were 350 investigations now underway, and I wonder what those investigations cover. Do they cover drugs and chemicals? We know that phenylephrine are found in sprays, cold tablets and so forth and that if a person uses hypertension pills, or pills for high blood pressure, he may get into serious trouble. I wonder how much we know about these things, if our testing is accurate and how many places we have where those substances can be accurately tested so that we can be sure of the results.
DDT can be found in large fish and in beef. However, if fatty parts are trimmed off, the amount of DDT will naturally be cut down. Freshwater fish are loaded with contamination, and we must keep these things in mind.
Cattle drink water from streams and creeks where DDT, insecticides and other chemicals are found. They wash into the water. The cattle drink that water, and yet the tests show a lower concentration in cows' milk than that found in mother's milk. Mothers should surely be protected more than animals. Do we have laboratory facilities for tests? In view of the fact that only one in four mothers nurse, would it not be wise to test them all and if necessary resort to cows' milk?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) has raised a number of questions, and I am quite sure we will read the record at a later date and respond to them. In the meantime, I would like to respond to the specific question the hon. member raised on December 14, 1977.
At that time the hon. member asked the minister whether her department was doing anything to provide any information to expectant or nursing mothers about diets which are low in pesticides and other chemical contaminants. In responding to this question the following points can be made. The information from several years of monitoring indicates that the amounts of pesticide in the total diet are much lower than those which have been set as the maximum safe level by the World Health Organization. For example, the amount of DDT in the total diet in 1974 was found to be only 0.5 per cent of the acceptable daily intake as set out by the World Health Organization.
Pesticides and other organic contaminants tend to accumulate in fatty foods. The Department of National Health and Welfare advocates the adoption by the public of a prudent diet which emphasizes consumption of increased amounts of fruits, vegetables and whole grain cereals and decreased amounts of sugar and fat. We encourage also the substitution of low fat milk and other similar modified products for conventional high fat items. Such a diet would be expected to contain reduced levels of fat soluble pesticides and other chemical contaminants.
Women of child-bearing age living in the Great Lakes system, including the St. Lawrence River valley, are advised to exercise caution in the consumption of locally caught game fish such as coho and Chinook salmon, eels and catfish. Only an occasional meal of locally caught fish of these species should be consumed by women of child-bearing age from the geographical areas mentioned. The forementioned Canadian guideline of two parts per million PCBs-polychloro biphenyls-for fish is the strictest in the world to our knowledge, and is carefully monitored by the fisheries and marine services branch of the Department of Fisheries and the Environment. Canadians can therefore be assured that commercial fish does not contain unsafe levels of PCBs.
An insert providing informative warning information for women of child-bearing age is being prepared for inclusion with the March 1978 family allowance cheques. This information will provide general dietary advice and specific information about reducing dietary fat intake.
I should like to point out to the hon. member that, as he asked a number of questions subsequent to the one on December 14, I will undertake on behalf of the minister to see that a letter is sent to him setting out what the department is doing on the matters he has raised which are very important.

Mr. Speaker, last January 27 I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) to get information from the Ontario Minister of Education about the conditions required to make French an official language in that province. I must recall that Ontario Premier William Davis wrote recently, and I quote:
The Ontario government does not intend at the present time to take any step to make French an official language of the province.
That rather startling announcement contains two notions that seem conflicting at first glance. It represents a categorical and absolute refusal. One remains temporarily shocked and stunned by its apparent finality. However, the Ontario premier did not close the door completely. He said: Not at the present time.
Such a statement makes us believe that the government of Ontario might change its mind if the situation evolved and that it would indeed agree to change its position if certain approaches were made. What would be those circumstances, those conditions, those prerequisites? I would like to say in passing that apparently some members have blamed me for my intervention in the House last Friday, perhaps because I was dealing with an issue concerning the province of Ontario. However, my intervention was valid and honest. I do not consider that I have narrow responsibilities as a member. I do not think I should deal only with problems concerning my riding in New Brunswick or other Atlantic provinces. I have the right and the privilege and even the duty and the intention of intervening to a greater degree in all questions pertaining to the fate of French Canadians everywhere across my country and of doing so beyond artificial barriers represented by jurisdictions. I challenge all other provinces to do as much for the two official language groups as has been done in the province of New Brunswick since the sixties under the government of Louis Robichaud and to a certain degree under the present administration.
In my opinion, the two linguistic communities of New Brunswick deserve greater credit for their achievements even if there is still a lot of progress to be made in such sectors as language, schools, services, than for instance Quebeckers who so far have gone through a smooth evolution under the umbrella of constitutional guarantees.
When Premier Davis states that he has no intention of taking any step to make French an official language and adds in the same breath specifying that such is his intention "at the present time", I feel as indignant and outraged as the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) himself felt. Yet I still hope and seriously believe that the Ontario government is willing to make some concessions. This is why I am asking the Secretary of State to look into it, to negotiate, to improve the dialogue. Is it Bill 101 in Quebec that Mr. Davis finds shocking? Is it the proposal made by Mr. Rene Levesque at the St. Andrews conference that is bothering him? Let him speak out frankly, let his education minister reveal the abcess so it may be lanced right now, but for goodness's sake let us not put in the balance the cultural life and language of Franco-Ontarians. Let them

January 31, 1978
Adjournment Debate
grant French official status in Ontario. It would be like pouring oil on a tormented sea, but above all it would amount to a demonstration of equity and justice.
The lame excuse that Ontario does not now have the resources to provide the required services which would automatically be needed once French gained official status is an easy way out.
That point was made recently by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Young) when answering a question put by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). Fie referred to the serious administrative impact of support personnel, not to mention the fact that in some provinces a start would have to be made from scratch. He was referring of course to the judicial area, our Canadian courts.
Time and good will can in my view overcome such obstacles. The province of New Brunswick has still less resources than Ontario, however, it did not wait for everything to be in place and perfectly developed to act. At this point in our history, in these times of emergency, Ontario has a unique opportunity! I am convinced the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) will spare neither time nor effort to offer his most sincere co-operation, with the rather significant federal resources, to encourage that province to take the next logical step. This would be a gesture so significant it would raise new hopes for the future of our country among those most depressed by the current situation.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PRIME MINISTER'S KNOWLEDGE THAT SOVIET SATELLITE CONTAINED NUCLEAR PACKAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the events of the past week made us look again at the provisions we have made for space exploration and the use of outer space. In questioning the minister involved last week, it became apparent there are major gaps in the system of international treaties governing outer space. Three aspects or the recent events seem to be of particular importance in highlighting these gaps.
First, the Soviet Union co-operated with us and earlier with the United States only after they were requested to do so. Second, the Soviet Union acted on a bilateral basis in this affair, apparently making no contacts with international organizations. Thus, only those countries which the United States or the Soviet Union chose to inform had advance warning of the danger. The satellite fell over an area which is not only sparsely populated, but in a country which eventually knew that a dangerous satellite was in trouble and which therefore had made some slight preparation.
Finally, in the search which is being conducted, the entire cost is up to now being borne by Canada and the United States, unless U.S.S.R. asks for the return of the debris under the provisions of article 5 of Treaty 1975 No. 6, the agreement on the return of objects launched into outer space. This section can and has been misinterpreted, I believe, in that article 5 states that expenses incurred in fulfilling obligations to recover and return the space object or its component parts under paragraphs 2 and 3 shall be borne by the launching authority. However, paragraphs 2 and 3, the operative parts, contain the words "contingent upon the requisition by the launching authority". So if the U.S.S.R. does not ask for the debris back it will not be liable for the cost of recovering the same. I presume it must have done so because yesterday the minister said the Soviet Union would meet its responsibilities.
[DOT]	(2232)
These circumstances are the consequence of some basic shortcomings in the treaties which deal with problems which could arise from mankind's use of space. The agreements all fail to take into account two important facts. First, while banning "any objects carrying nuclear weapons", the treaty-makers did not prohibit the inclusion of dangerous amounts of fissionable material in satellites. The treaty-makers seem not to have realized that a situation could arise in which an unarmed satellite would, upon re-entry, pose a threat to a wide area, that is, a threat apart from the immediate physical damage caused by impact.
In the second place they do not take into account the rapid advances in satellite tracking technology and thus ignore the opportunities presented by the fact that there are often significant lengths of time in which to prepare ourselves before a satellite re-enters the atmosphere. Neither do the accords take cognizance of the coming of the space shuttle orbiters. These should be in operation in two years' time and within five years

they should be of great help in relieving us from the dangers we were facing last week.
The remedy for these shortcomings lies, I believe, in simple amendments to the treaties themselves. First, the convention on the registration of objects launched into outer space should be amended so that, in addition to the basic orbital parameters, the launching states would be required to notify the Secretary General of the UN of the inclusion of any fissionable material in a satellite. Perhaps in order to avoid difficulties and red tape in connection with safe scientific experiments there should be some minimum amount provided for, such as 100 grams, below which no notification would be required. An exemption of this sort could no doubt be arranged after discussion with the technical experts.
The second change which should be made is an addition requiring the launching state to notify the Secretary General of the United Nations whether any satellite re-entering the atmosphere contains any material, fissionable, chemical or biological, which could present a safety threat if it reached earth. Notification to this effect should be made as soon as it is ascertained that the satellite is likely to re-enter the atmosphere. The Secretary General in turn would notify any state over which the satellite was passing.
Third, once a satellite has been classified by this method as potentially dangerous, states with satellite tracking capability-presumably the United States and the U.S.S.R.-would be required to keep the Secretary General informed of the expected time and location of re-entry. Once a location could be predicted, the Secretary General and the heads of the states affected are to be informed.
Finally, reasonable costs of searching for and containing the contamination, even if the search is only to confirm that the satellite was entirely consumed during re-entry, should be treated as damages under the existing convention of international liability for damage caused by space objects. This would make it possible to recover such costs. In addition, article XXI of Treaty No. 1 would permit the affected state to seek assistance from the launching state in this search and containment operation.
Taken together, these suggestions would, if implemented, give us a safer world, one in which the risks to the population at large inherent in space exploration and use would be reduced. The government should learn from its experience of the ad hoc and frequently inefficient train of communication evident in the past week's crisis and press vigorously for the changes I have outlined.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated to the hon. member, in response to his question concerning the briefings at NORAD during his visit there in late December, that he was advised that NORAD headquarters were monitoring all the satellites and other man-made objects in space and that the headquarters were aware of the situation. Fie also stated that they went into some detail at his briefings which he did not think it was appropriate for him to disclose.
The hon. member must know from the responses to various questions given by the Prime Minister and the Ministry of National Defence that Canada and the United States have had complete and harmonious co-operation on all aspects dealing with the Cosmos satellite. Before January 20, 1978 when the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) were briefed on the probability of the Cosmos landing on earth and a possibility that it may be in Canada, there was no requirement for a detailed disposition of the Cosmos as it was not apparent that its disorientation would affect North America. In fact, it was considered that it may land in the south Atlantic or sometime later in the year, probably in the month of April 1978.
The Minister of National Defence and the Chief of the Defence Staff have openly and frankly reported on all aspects of this event and continue to do so the minute new information is available. They will continue to do so until the matter has been finalized. At this time, the Canadian and American armed forces and Department of Energy, Mines and Resources' officials and other agencies and officials concerned with the operation continue to operate in close co-operation with the forces' information officials in Edmonton and are providing details of the operation to the news media as soon as communications permit.
The Canadian forces' officials were informed of the disorientation of the Cosmos as early as September 1977. Details of its progress were reported as its disposition changed. At each stage, higher levels of authority were advised, culminating with the Minister of National Defence and the Prime Minister several days prior to the final plunge. As the Minister of National Defence has stated several times, he is satisfied that he received timely information on the Cosmos through proper channels following recognized procedures.
I am sure the hon. member will appreciate that he has made other representations as well which will be taken into consideration by the Minister of National Defence and the Prime Minister.
